papers.research_question: How do deep neural networks for speech recognition untangle task-relevant information (e.g., words, phonemes) and discard nuisance variations (e.g., speaker identity) across layers and over time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that deep speech recognition models untangle task-relevant auditory class manifolds (e.g., words, phonemes) and discard nuisance variations (e.g., speaker identity) across layers, and that this untangling emerges from training and is consistent across different network architectures.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks for speech recognition untangle auditory class manifolds in a manner analogous to vision networks, and geometric analysis of representations reveals how invariant speech recognition is achieved.
papers.key_findings:
Word manifolds become more linearly separable (higher manifold capacity) in later layers of both CNN and Deep Speech 2 models.
Higher-level concepts such as phonemes and parts-of-speech also become untangled in later layers, though to a lesser extent than words.
Speaker information (speaker manifolds) is discarded in models trained for speech recognition, as evidenced by decreased manifold capacity for speaker manifolds in later layers.
Temporal untangling occurs over time steps in recurrent layers, with word separability peaking near the word's temporal location.
The untangling is task-dependent: models trained for speaker recognition untangle speaker manifolds but not word manifolds.
future_direction: Theory-driven geometric analysis of representation untangling in tasks with temporal structure.
Search for the mechanistic relation between the network architecture, learned parameters, and structure of the stimuli via the lens of geometry.
Study of competing vs. synergistic tasks enabled by the geometric analysis tool.
papers.abstract: Encouraged by the success of deep neural networks on a variety of visual tasks, much theoretical and experimental work has been aimed at understanding and interpreting how vision networks operate. Meanwhile, deep neural networks have also achieved impressive performance in audio processing applications, both as sub-components of larger systems and as complete end-to-end systems by themselves. Despite their empirical successes, comparatively little is understood about how these audio models accomplish these tasks. In this work, we employ a recently developed statistical mechanical theory that connects geometric properties of network representations and the separability of classes to probe how information is untangled within neural networks trained to recognize speech. We observe that speaker-specific nuisance variations are discarded by the network's hierarchy, whereas task-relevant properties such as words and phonemes are untangled in later layers. Higher level concepts such as parts-of-speech and context dependence also emerge in the later layers of the network. Finally, we find that the deep representations carry out significant temporal untangling by efficiently extracting task-relevant features at each time step of the computation. Taken together, these findings shed light on how deep auditory models process time dependent input signals to achieve invariant speech recognition, and show how different concepts emerge through the layers of the network.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How do individual CNN features from all layers behave for feature extraction and transfer learning, and can both presence and absence of feature activations be informative?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both presence and absence, and that convolutional layers are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the behavior of CNN features for feature extraction, showing that both presence and absence of features are informative, and that convolutional layers are more general than previously thought, which can be exploited for knowledge representation and reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their absence, providing a different information modality, especially in fine-grained datasets.
Features from the last convolutional layer and fully connected layers are highly specific, while other convolutional layers convey more variate information.
For certain tasks, convolutional features outperform fully-connected features at discriminating labels, indicating low-level layers are more general and discriminant.
Low and middle level features have similar behavior across datasets, suggesting they can be used for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly related to the similarity of the task with the original training task and the width of the task spectrum.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Create Cross-Modal Task Representations
papers.research_question: Do vision-language models (VLMs) map conceptually equivalent inputs (across modalities and formats) into a shared task representation?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs map conceptually equivalent inputs (text examples, image examples, instructions) into a shared task representation, and cross-modal patching of this single task vector can effectively transfer task information across modalities.
papers.conclusion: VLMs map inputs into a shared task representation space regardless of specification modality or format, and cross-modal patching is an effective method for analyzing and utilizing these representations.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs struggle with cross-modal few-shot prompting (input regurgitation), but cross-modal patching of a task vector resolves this issue and often outperforms unimodal baselines.
Task vectors can be transferred from a base language model (LLM) to its fine-tuned vision-language counterpart (VLM), indicating representational re-use.
Task vectors can be defined solely from instructions, and ensembling instruction- and example-based vectors improves sample efficiency.
VLMs map text and image examples (and instructions) to similar task vectors, despite maintaining distinct image and text embeddings in the context.
The token representation evolution during in-context learning follows three phases (input, task, answer) that are shared across text and image ICL.
papers.limitation:
The work shows that VLMs learn cross-modal task representations but lacks a definitive explanation for why.
The reliability of these models remains a limitation; task adaptation often comes at the cost of accuracy, requiring further stress testing before deployment in critical applications.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) can handle many tasks within a single model, yet the representations that enable this capability remain opaque. We find that VLMs align conceptually equivalent inputs into a shared task vector, which is invariant to modality (text, image) and format (examples, instruction), and may simplify VLM processing. We measure this alignment via cross-modal transfer -- the ability of a task vector derived in one modality to trigger the correct generation in another -- on a range of tasks and model architectures. Although the task vector is highly compressed, we find that this single vector outperforms prompting the model with the full task information, unique to this cross-modal case. Furthermore, we show that task vectors can be transferred from a base language model to its fine-tuned vision-language counterpart, and that they can be derived solely from instructions without the need for examples. Taken together, our findings shed light on how VLMs internally process task information, and how they map different modalities into common semantic representations. Project page: https://vlm-cross-modal-reps.github.io.

papers.title: Disentangled Representations in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations in neural models that are interpretable, reusable, and performant, without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods (DC-IGN and CFN) for learning disentangled representations in graphics and computation, which are interpretable, reusable, and performant without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled representations are valuable for interpretability and reuse, and the proposed methods (DC-IGN and CFN) are effective in learning such representations in the domains of graphics and computation.
papers.key_findings:
DC-IGN can learn a disentangled graphics code for 3D faces and chairs, enabling novel view synthesis and re-rendering under different lighting and pose conditions.
CFN can disentangle computational tasks, factorize a multitask learning problem, and is practically immune to catastrophic forgetting.
Explicit disentanglement training is critical for novel-view reconstruction compared to entangled representations.
The decoder in DC-IGN can function as a 3D rendering engine, indicating a truly disentangled representation.
CFN achieves disentanglement with no performance penalty and with fewer parameters than a traditional feedforward network.
papers.limitation:
The current formulation of SGVB is restricted to continuous latent variables, but real-world scenes may require discrete distributions.
Scaling to more complex scenes may require deeper architectures.
The decoder network might be replaced by a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained model-based inference.
future_direction: Experiment with deeper architectures to handle more complex scenes and object categories.
Extend the model to handle discrete distributions or to a recurrent setting.
Use importance-weighted autoencoders to capture more complex probabilistic structure.
Replace the decoder with a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained inference.
Explore multi-step CFN for deeper computations and curricula.
Investigate non-differentiable functions in CFN and hierarchical computation.
Unify the two approaches for unsupervised inference of factors of variation in videos.
papers.abstract: Representation learning is the foundation for the recent success of neural network models. However, the distributed representations generated by neural networks are far from ideal. Due to their highly entangled nature, they are di cult to reuse and interpret, and they do a poor job of capturing the sparsity which is present in real- world transformations. In this paper, I describe methods for learning disentangled representations in the two domains of graphics and computation. These methods allow neural methods to learn representations which are easy to interpret and reuse, yet they incur little or no penalty to performance. In the Graphics section, I demonstrate the ability of these methods to infer the generating parameters of images and rerender those images under novel conditions. In the Computation section, I describe a model which is able to factorize a multitask learning problem into subtasks and which experiences no catastrophic forgetting. Together these techniques provide the tools to design a wide range of models that learn disentangled representations and better model the factors of variation in the real world.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Unsupervised learning in images and audio to produce neural receptive fields: a primer and accessible notebook
papers.research_question: How can unsupervised learning, specifically Independent Component Analysis (ICA), model early sensory processing in vision and audition, and how does it compare to Principal Component Analysis (PCA)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a consolidated review and demonstration of Independent Component Analysis (ICA) as an efficient neural coding scheme for early sensory processing, showing that ICA produces receptive field models similar to physiological ones for natural inputs, and provides an accessible Jupyter notebook for educational and research purposes.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICA is a neurally appropriate efficient coding strategy for natural sensory data, and the provided Jupyter notebook demonstrates the principle in an accessible way for educational and research purposes.
papers.key_findings:
ICA produces filters resembling biological receptive fields (Gabor-like for vision, gammatone-like for audition) when applied to natural inputs, while PCA does not.
Non-natural inputs do not yield neural-like filters with ICA, indicating that both the coding objective and the natural statistics of the input are necessary.
The same five-step computational strategy can model early sensory processing across modalities (grayscale, color, audio) with only a change in inputs.
papers.limitation:
The demonstration uses a relatively small dataset of images from the internet which can bias the results.
Evaluation is by visual comparison only, without empirical or statistical evaluation.
Only grayscale, color, and audio modalities are demonstrated; video and binocular modalities are not included.
future_direction: Include video and binocular modalities in the notebook.
Use larger datasets and empirical evaluation of derived filters.
Explore the use of ICA filters as pre-trained features in deep learning models.
papers.abstract: Abstract Sensory processing relies on efficient computation driven by a combination of low-level unsupervised, statistical structural learning, and high-level task-dependent learning. In the earliest stages of sensory processing, sparse and independent coding strategies are capable of modeling neural processing using the same coding strategy with only a change in the input (e.g., grayscale images, color images, and audio). We present a consolidated review of Independent Component Analysis (ICA) as an efficient neural coding scheme with the ability to model early visual and auditory neural processing. We created a self-contained, accessible Jupyter notebook using Python to demonstrate the efficient coding principle for different modalities following a consistent five-step strategy. For each modality, derived receptive field models from natural and non-natural inputs are contrasted, demonstrating how neural codes are not produced when the inputs sufficiently deviate from those animals were evolved to process. Additionally, the demonstration shows that ICA produces more neurally-appropriate receptive field models than those based on common compression strategies, such as Principal Component Analysis. The five-step strategy not only produces neural-like models but also promotes reuse of code to emphasize the input-agnostic nature where each modality can be modeled with only a change in inputs. This notebook can be used to readily observe the links between unsupervised machine learning strategies and early sensory neuroscience, improving our understanding of flexible data-driven neural development in nature and future applications.

papers.title: Latent Space Translation via Semantic Alignment
papers.research_question: How can latent spaces of different neural networks be translated to enable zero-shot stitching without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Latent spaces of different neural networks can be translated via simple algebraic transformations (e.g., orthogonal) estimated from a set of corresponding anchor points, enabling zero-shot stitching across architectures and modalities without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Latent space translation via simple algebraic transformations is an effective and efficient approach for zero-shot model compositionality across diverse neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The transformation between latent spaces of different networks is mostly orthogonal, enabling effective translation via Procrustes analysis.
The method works in cross-modality settings, allowing zero-shot stitching of text encoders with image decoders and vice versa.
The translation method is effective for both classification and reconstruction (autoencoding) tasks.
Performance improves with the number of anchor points but saturates with a relatively small set.
The method outperforms naive absolute and relative representation baselines in stitching accuracy.
papers.limitation: The optimal number of anchor points and factors affecting latent space compatibility (e.g., intrinsic dimension) require further exploration.
future_direction: Investigating the optimal number of anchor points for different tasks and datasets.
Exploring factors linked to latent space compatibility, such as intrinsic dimension.
Studying trade-offs between anchor set granularity and its condition number.
papers.abstract: While different neural models often exhibit latent spaces that are alike when exposed to semantically related data, this intrinsic similarity is not always immediately discernible. Towards a better understanding of this phenomenon, our work shows how representations learned from these neural modules can be translated between different pre-trained networks via simpler transformations than previously thought. An advantage of this approach is the ability to estimate these transformations using standard, well-understood algebraic procedures that have closed-form solutions. Our method directly estimates a transformation between two given latent spaces, thereby enabling effective stitching of encoders and decoders without additional training. We extensively validate the adaptability of this translation procedure in different experimental settings: across various trainings, domains, architectures (e.g., ResNet, CNN, ViT), and in multiple downstream tasks (classification, reconstruction). Notably, we show how it is possible to zero-shot stitch text encoders and vision decoders, or vice-versa, yielding surprisingly good classification performance in this multimodal setting.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: How do Multimodal Foundation Models Encode Text and Speech? An Analysis of Cross-Lingual and Cross-Modal Representations
papers.research_question: How do multimodal foundation models encode text and speech? Specifically, how do they represent semantically equivalent sentences across languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual and cross-modal representations in multimodal foundation models, finding that cross-modal similarity increases over layers, length adaptation helps but is limited to high-resource languages, speech has larger cross-lingual differences than text, and the modality gap is often larger than the language gap.
papers.conclusion: While multimodal foundation models present a unified architecture, they do not inherently create fully unified semantic representations. Representational gaps such as speech-text length mismatches, weak representations for low-resource languages, and tokenizer bottlenecks persist.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers which are specialized for text or speech processing.
Length adaptation mechanisms (e.g., pooling, Q-Former) are crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap, but their effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages.
Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text, likely due to greater variability in acoustic features and recording conditions.
For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations (Seamless, SALMONN), the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.
Tokenizer fragmentation for languages with diverse scripts (e.g., in SALMONN) leads to inflated initial similarity scores that drop in subsequent layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the FLEURS dataset, which is created from Wikipedia texts, may limit generalizability to other domains like informal or spoken texts.
The study focuses only on speech and text modalities; exploring other modalities like images is out of scope.
Only three multimodal foundation models are analyzed; newer models like Qwen-Audio and Llama 3 are not covered.
Six of the 30 analyzed languages are not shared between SONAR and the other models, creating a non-fully overlapping experimental setup.
Findings are based on intrinsic analyses (SVCCA on activations); other explainability methods or downstream task performance could provide complementary insights.
papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models aim to create a unified representation space that abstracts away from surface features like language syntax or modality differences. To investigate this, we study the internal representations of three recent models, analyzing the model activations from semantically equivalent sentences across languages in the text and speech modalities. Our findings reveal that: 1) Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers specialized at text and speech processing. 2) Length adaptation is crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap between text and speech, although current approaches' effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages. 3) Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text. 4) For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations, the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.

papers.title: Wider Networks Learn Better Features
papers.research_question: How does network width affect the features learned by neural networks, and do wider networks learn more transferable features for novel tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Wider networks learn more informative and transferable features in their hidden states, as visualized by activation atlases, leading to better performance when fine-tuning on novel tasks, even when test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.
papers.conclusion: Wider networks learn more informative features that are beneficial for transfer learning, even when original task performance is unchanged.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in wide networks do not learn interpretable features, but groups of neurons (via activation atlases) do.
Hidden states of wide networks contain more information about inputs than narrow networks, even when test accuracy on the original task is the same.
Fine-tuning a linear classifier on features from a wide network on a new task yields better performance than on narrow networks, even with the same original task accuracy.
The additional information in wide networks (e.g., translation information in translated MNIST) is preserved and useful for transfer.
The features learned by wide networks are distributed across neurons, not sparse.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters for wider networks (e.g., learning rate) might be tuned to improve performance on the original task, but this was not explored.
The experiments are conducted on relatively small datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) and network widths, not in the infinite width or lazy training regime.
future_direction: Explore the effect of network width on the performance of transfer learning algorithms like MAML.
Investigate feature learning in the infinite width limit and lazy training regime.
papers.abstract: Transferability of learned features between tasks can massively reduce the cost of training a neural network on a novel task. We investigate the effect of network width on learned features using activation atlases --- a visualization technique that captures features the entire hidden state responds to, as opposed to individual neurons alone. We find that, while individual neurons do not learn interpretable features in wide networks, groups of neurons do. In addition, the hidden state of a wide network contains more information about the inputs than that of a narrow network trained to the same test accuracy. Inspired by this observation, we show that when fine-tuning the last layer of a network on a new task, performance improves significantly as the width of the network is increased, even though test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep neural networks transfer layer-wise across different datasets and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks can be non-symmetric, is more influenced by dataset/task nature than architecture, and can quantify task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches in multi-task learning paradigms to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between two datasets or tasks can be non-symmetric.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to neural network architecture.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers.
Representations learned on more general datasets (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific datasets (e.g., SVHN).
papers.abstract: Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: Promoting cross-modal representations to improve multimodal foundation models for physiological signals
papers.research_question: Which pretraining strategies are most effective for multimodal foundation models with diverse physiological signals, and how can cross-modal representation learning be encouraged?
papers.core_contribution: Adding input modality drop to multimodal masked autoencoding (MultiMAE) pretraining improves cross-modal representation learning and downstream task performance for diverse physiological signals.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal foundation models are effective for physiological signals, and explicitly promoting cross-modal reconstruction through input modality drop improves representation quality and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained multimodal models develop representations that support a diverse set of downstream tasks in physiological data.
Adding input modality drop to MAE pretraining improves downstream task performance compared to standard MultiMAE.
Late fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are more variable in performance and underperform MAE with modality drop on aggregate.
MAE with input modality drop encourages cross-modal fusion in attention weights and leads to more distributed tuning of embedding units across modalities.
The learned representations are effective even with limited labeled data.
papers.limitation: Making comparisons with other datasets would be additionally informative, since multimodal fusion strategies are often dependent on the dataset and task at hand.
future_direction: Developing a large range of downstream tasks to better understand the strengths of different pretraining strategies.
Developing new formulations of contrastive learning that may improve task performance for multimodal biosignals.
papers.abstract: Many healthcare applications are inherently multimodal, involving several physiological signals. As sensors for these signals become more common, improving machine learning methods for multimodal healthcare data is crucial. Pretraining foundation models is a promising avenue for success. However, methods for developing foundation models in healthcare are still in early exploration and it is unclear which pretraining strategies are most effective given the diversity of physiological signals. This is partly due to challenges in multimodal health data: obtaining data across many patients is difficult and costly, there is a lot of inter-subject variability, and modalities are often heterogeneously informative across downstream tasks. Here, we explore these challenges in the PhysioNet 2018 dataset. We use a masked autoencoding objective to pretrain a multimodal model. We show that the model learns representations that can be linearly probed for a diverse set of downstream tasks. We hypothesize that cross-modal reconstruction objectives are important for successful multimodal training, as they encourage the model to integrate information across modalities. We demonstrate that modality dropout in the input space improves performance across downstream tasks. We also find that late-fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are less effective across multiple tasks. Finally, we analyze the model's representations, showing that attention weights become more cross-modal and temporally aligned with our pretraining strategy. The learned embeddings also become more distributed in terms of the modalities encoded by each unit. Overall, our work demonstrates the utility of multimodal foundation models with health data, even across diverse physiological data sources. We further argue that explicit methods for inducing cross-modality may enhance multimodal pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between\n Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep networks transfer between different datasets and tasks, and what factors influence this transferability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks is non-symmetric, influenced more by dataset nature than network architecture, and can serve as a proxy for task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The observations highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches to designing systems for multiple tasks to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between datasets can be non-symmetric, e.g., features from CIFAR datasets are more transferable to SVHN than vice versa.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to the neural network architecture.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers across different tasks.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Representations learned on more general classes (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific classes (e.g., SVHN digits).
papers.abstract:
Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed
representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and
transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as
transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this
notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge
across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of
representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some
interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations of Text by Masking Transformers
papers.research_question: Is it possible to learn disentangled representations by identifying existing subnetworks within pretrained models that encode distinct, complementary aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to learn disentangled representations by learning binary masks over the weights or hidden activations of a pretrained transformer (BERT), identifying sparse subnetworks that encode specific aspects while minimizing information about others.
papers.conclusion: Masking is an effective approach for disentangling representations in pretrained transformers without fine-tuning, offering benefits for model robustness and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Learning binary masks over BERT's weights or hidden activations can disentangle representations of factors like sentiment/genre, toxicity/dialect, and syntax/semantics.
The masking method performs as well as or better than existing disentanglement methods based on variational autoencoders and adversarial training.
Disentangled representations via masking are more robust to shifts in spurious correlations between attributes in the training data.
The discovered subnetworks suggest semantic information is captured in higher BERT layers, while syntactic information is in lower layers.
The method achieves competitive performance on main tasks while reducing leakage of non-target attributes.
papers.abstract: Representations from large pretrained models such as BERT encode a range of features into monolithic vectors, affording strong predictive accuracy across a range of downstream tasks. In this paper we explore whether it is possible to learn disentangled representations by identifying existing subnetworks within pretrained models that encode distinct, complementary aspects. Concretely, we learn binary masks over transformer weights or hidden units to uncover subsets of features that correlate with a specific factor of variation; this eliminates the need to train a disentangled model from scratch for a particular task. We evaluate this method with respect to its ability to disentangle representations of sentiment from genre in movie reviews, toxicity from dialect in Tweets, and syntax from semantics. By combining masking with magnitude pruning we find that we can identify sparse subnetworks within BERT that strongly encode particular aspects (e.g., semantics) while only weakly encoding others (e.g., syntax). Moreover, despite only learning masks, disentanglement-via-masking performs as well as -and often better thanpreviously proposed methods based on variational autoencoders and adversarial training.

papers.title: Words That Make Language Models Perceive
papers.research_question: Can explicit sensory prompting (e.g., 'see' or 'hear') surface latent multimodal structure in text-only large language models, bringing their internal representations into closer alignment with specialist vision and audio encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight sensory prompting (e.g., asking a text-only LLM to 'see' or 'hear') can steer its internal representations to align more closely with those of specialist vision or audio encoders, and this alignment improves with generation length and model size.
papers.conclusion: Sensory prompting can actively steer text-only LLMs into perceptually grounded representations at inference time, supporting the view that LLMs implicitly encode multimodal regularities and that their representations can be controlled via prompt engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Generative representations (from autoregressive continuations) yield higher alignment with sensory encoders than single-pass embeddings.
Sensory cues (SEE/HEAR) steer generative representations to increase alignment with the corresponding modality encoder and decrease alignment with the mismatched one.
Alignment increases with generation length up to a point, after which semantic drift can reduce it.
Larger models exhibit higher alignment under sensory prompting and show clearer separation between modality-specific representations.
Sensory prompting improves performance on visual question answering (VQA) in a text-only setting, indicating practical benefits for perceptual grounding.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses primarily on lightweight cues like 'see' and 'hear' and does not explore broader variation in instruction phrasing that could better elicit perceptual framing.
Potential for prompt optimization is noted, but alignment evaluation is computationally expensive, making systematic prompt search challenging.
Overly long generations (e.g., 512 tokens) can lead to semantic drift and reduce alignment gains.
The degree to which alignment can be improved is not fully explored.
future_direction: Exploring broader variation in instruction phrasing to better elicit perceptual framing.
Optimizing prompts to maximize alignment, though computationally challenging.
Further study of layer-wise effects and why averaging across layers yields higher alignment.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained purely on text ostensibly lack any direct perceptual experience, yet their internal representations are implicitly shaped by multimodal regularities encoded in language. We test the hypothesis that explicit sensory prompting can surface this latent structure, bringing a text-only LLM into closer representational alignment with specialist vision and audio encoders. When a sensory prompt tells the model to 'see' or 'hear', it cues the model to resolve its next-token predictions as if they were conditioned on latent visual or auditory evidence that is never actually supplied. Our findings reveal that lightweight prompt engineering can reliably activate modality-appropriate representations in purely text-trained LLMs.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Understanding the Emergence of Multimodal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: When and why does alignment emerge implicitly? Is alignment a reliable indicator of performance?
papers.core_contribution: The emergence of alignment and its relationship with task performance depend on data characteristics such as heterogeneity and the balance between redundant and unique information; alignment is not universally beneficial.
papers.conclusion: Alignment may not be universally beneficial; its impact on performance varies depending on dataset and task characteristics, guiding practitioners on when to pursue alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum achievable alignment decreases as the level of unique information increases.
Alignment correlates with performance in datasets with high redundancy, but this relationship breaks down when uniqueness dominates.
Increasing model capacity improves alignment only when modalities are redundant and fails when uniqueness is high.
The correlation between alignment and performance varies across datasets and tasks, indicating that alignment is not a reliable performance indicator in all cases.
Data heterogeneity negatively affects the level of achievable alignment.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a simplified two-modality setting; generalization to more modalities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Extending the study to more than two modalities.
Investigating alignment in dynamic or sequential multimodal tasks.
Exploring the role of alignment in multimodal fusion architectures.
papers.abstract: Multimodal representation learning is fundamentally about transforming incomparable modalities into comparable representations. While prior research primarily focused on explicitly aligning these representations through targeted learning objectives and model architectures, a recent line of work has found that independently trained unimodal models of increasing scale and performance can become implicitly aligned with each other. These findings raise fundamental questions regarding the emergence of aligned representations in multimodal learning. Specifically: (1) when and why does alignment emerge implicitly? and (2) is alignment a reliable indicator of performance? Through a comprehensive empirical investigation, we demonstrate that both the emergence of alignment and its relationship with task performance depend on several critical data characteristics. These include, but are not necessarily limited to, the degree of similarity between the modalities and the balance between redundant and unique information they provide for the task. Our findings suggest that alignment may not be universally beneficial; rather, its impact on performance varies depending on the dataset and task. These insights can help practitioners determine whether increasing alignment between modalities is advantageous or, in some cases, detrimental to achieving optimal performance. Code is released at https://github.com/MeganTj/multimodal_alignment.

papers.title: Deconstructing multimodality: visual properties and visual context in human semantic processing
papers.research_question: Whether differentiating between internal visual properties and external visual context is beneficial compared to learning visual representations from complete images for decoding brain activity associated with noun meanings.
papers.core_contribution: Multimodal semantic models that differentiate between internal and external visual features correlate with human neural semantic representations, and internal visual features are most important for decoding brain activity associated with concrete nouns.
papers.conclusion: Internal visual features are superior for decoding brain activity associated with concrete nouns, and automatic object detection techniques can produce high-quality visual representations, reducing reliance on manually annotated datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Models using internal visual features (VIS-INTERNAL) outperform those using external or whole-image features in decoding brain activity.
Multimodal models combining linguistic and visual information (MM-INTERNAL, MM-EXTERNAL) perform better than visual-only models.
The combined multimodal model (MM-COMBINED) outperforms the whole-image multimodal model.
Models using automatically annotated images perform on par with those using manually annotated images, demonstrating the utility of automatic object detection.
papers.abstract: Multimodal semantic models that extend linguistic representations with additional perceptual input have proved successful in a range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Recent research has successfully used neural methods to automatically create visual representations for words. However, these works have extracted visual features from complete images, and have not examined how different kinds of visual information impact performance. In contrast, we construct multimodal models that differentiate between internal visual properties of the objects and their external visual context. We evaluate the models on the task of decoding brain activity associated with the meanings of nouns, demonstrating their advantage over those based on complete images.

papers.title: Cross-Entropy Is All You Need To Invert the Data Generating Process
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether cross-entropy-based supervised learning can invert the data generating process and recover ground-truth latent variables up to a linear transformation under a cluster-centric data generating process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that under a cluster-centric data generating process, cross-entropy-based supervised learning can recover ground-truth latent variables up to a linear transformation, providing a theoretical explanation for the linear representations observed in deep learning models.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that cross-entropy minimization in supervised learning can invert the data generating process and recover latent variables up to linear transformations, offering a unifying theory for the effectiveness of supervised deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Under the proposed cluster-centric DGP, DIET (parametric instance discrimination) identifies both latent variables and cluster vectors up to linear transformations.
Supervised classification with cross-entropy loss also recovers latent variables up to a linear transformation under the same DGP.
Empirical results on synthetic data confirm the theoretical identifiability when assumptions are met.
On the DisLib benchmark, simple classification tasks recover latent structures up to linear transformations.
On ImageNet-X, pretrained models encode representations that allow linear decoding of proxy factors of variation.
papers.limitation: The theory relies on specific assumptions about the DGP, such as the vMF distribution and cluster structure, which may not hold in real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the theory to more general distributions beyond vMF
Investigating identifiability in the presence of label noise
Applying the insights to improve self-supervised learning algorithms
papers.abstract: Supervised learning has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, yet a comprehensive theory explaining its effectiveness remains elusive. Empirical phenomena, such as neural analogy-making and the linear representation hypothesis, suggest that supervised models can learn interpretable factors of variation in a linear fashion. Recent advances in self-supervised learning, particularly nonlinear Independent Component Analysis, have shown that these methods can recover latent structures by inverting the data generating process. We extend these identifiability results to parametric instance discrimination, then show how insights transfer to the ubiquitous setting of supervised learning with cross-entropy minimization. We prove that even in standard classification tasks, models learn representations of ground-truth factors of variation up to a linear transformation. We corroborate our theoretical contribution with a series of empirical studies. First, using simulated data matching our theoretical assumptions, we demonstrate successful disentanglement of latent factors. Second, we show that on DisLib, a widely-used disentanglement benchmark, simple classification tasks recover latent structures up to linear transformations. Finally, we reveal that models trained on ImageNet encode representations that permit linear decoding of proxy factors of variation. Together, our theoretical findings and experiments offer a compelling explanation for recent observations of linear representations, such as superposition in neural networks. This work takes a significant step toward a cohesive theory that accounts for the unreasonable effectiveness of supervised deep learning.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
