papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Understanding trained CNNs by indexing neuron selectivity
papers.research_question: How can we understand and visualize the internal representations of Convolutional Neural Networks by indexing neuron selectivity to specific properties like color and class?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to understand CNN internal representations by visualizing Neuron Features and quantifying neuron selectivity indexes for color and class, enabling the analysis of how features and classes are represented across layers.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully indexes neuron selectivity, showing how color and class representations are organized across CNN layers, with implications for understanding neural coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
Color selectivity is present in all convolutional layers, with 40% in conv1 and 30% in conv2, decreasing but still present in deeper layers.
Class selectivity increases with depth, with over 50% of neurons in conv5 having high class selectivity (index >0.6).
Neuron Feature visualization reveals clear shapes for some neurons and blurred features for others, suggesting different coding strategies.
The framework can identify specific neurons selective to colors or classes, such as a red-mushroom neuron in conv4 or dog-face neurons in conv5.
Color is important for object recognition, as grayscale images lead to higher classification errors.
future_direction: Apply indexes to different neural network architectures.
Define new selectivity indexes for shape, texture, or part detection.
Study relations between indexes.

papers.title: Semantic representations emerge in biologically inspired ensembles of cross-supervising neural networks
papers.research_question: Whether neural networks that receive different parts of the same input can supervise each other to form meaningful representations, without external supervision.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a biologically plausible framework (CLoSeR) for unsupervised representation learning where networks with small receptive fields cross-supervise each other, learning semantic representations that are easily decodable and comparable to supervised networks.
papers.conclusion: CLoSeR provides a biologically plausible algorithm for unsupervised learning of semantic representations by ensembles of cross-supervising networks, suggesting a mechanism for collective learning in the brain.
papers.key_findings:
CLoSeR networks learn semantic representations of images that are linearly separable and comparable to supervised networks.
Performance is optimal when each network sees a small fraction of the input (small receptive fields).
Sparse interaction graphs (e.g., rings) achieve near-optimal performance with fewer computations than all-to-all.
CLoSeR is effective for both MLP and Vision Transformer architectures.
Temporal variant TCLoSeR learns meaningful representations from neuronal population data.
papers.limitation: The model uses feedforward networks and gradient descent with backpropagation, which are not fully biologically plausible.
future_direction: Extend the algorithm to Recurrent Neural Networks for more biological relevance.
Develop more local and biological learning rules to replace backpropagation.
Explore scaled-up versions, more stimulus classes, and more intricate interaction graphs.
papers.abstract: Brains learn to represent information from a large set of stimuli, typically by weak supervision. Unsupervised learning is therefore a natural approach for exploring the design of biological neural networks and their computations. Accordingly, redundancy reduction has been suggested as a prominent design principle of neural encoding, but its ``mechanistic'' biological implementation is unclear. Analogously, unsupervised training of artificial neural networks yields internal representations that allow for accurate stimulus classification or decoding, but typically rely on biologically-implausible implementations. We suggest that interactions between parallel subnetworks in the brain may underlie such learning: we present a model of representation learning by ensembles of neural networks, where each network learns to encode stimuli into an abstract representation space by cross-supervising interactions with other networks, for inputs they receive simultaneously or in close temporal proximity. Aiming for biological plausibility, each network has a small ``receptive field'', thus receiving a fixed part of the external input, and the networks do not share weights. We find that for different types of network architectures, and for both visual or neuronal stimuli, these cross-supervising networks learn semantic representations that are easily decodable and that decoding accuracy is comparable to supervised networks -- both at the level of single networks and the ensemble. We further show that performance is optimal for small receptive fields, and that sparse connectivity between networks is nearly as accurate as all-to-all interactions, with far fewer computations. We thus suggest a sparsely interacting collective of cross-supervising networks as an algorithmic framework for representational learning and collective computation in the brain.

papers.title: Neural Encoding and Decoding at Scale
papers.research_question: How can we develop a unified, scalable model to capture the bidirectional relationship between neural activity and behavior, overcoming the limitation of existing approaches that focus exclusively on either encoding or decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NEDS, a multimodal, multi-task transformer model with a novel multi-task-masking strategy that unifies neural encoding and decoding, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both tasks and demonstrating emergent brain region predictability in its learned embeddings.
papers.conclusion: NEDS introduces a flexible and scalable paradigm for modeling the bidirectional relationship between neural activity and behavior, representing a step towards a foundation model of the brain that enables seamless translation between modalities.
papers.key_findings:
NEDS outperforms unimodal baselines and state-of-the-art models (POYO+, NDT2) in both neural encoding and decoding tasks when pretrained on multi-animal data and fine-tuned on held-out animals.
Pretraining NEDS across many animals (73) significantly improves performance on held-out animals compared to single-session training, demonstrating effective scaling.
The learned neuron embeddings from NEDS exhibit emergent properties, accurately predicting the brain region of each recording without explicit training, achieving 83% classification accuracy.
The multi-task-masking strategy (neural, behavioral, within-modality, cross-modal) is crucial for learning the bidirectional conditional expectations between neural activity and behavior.
Encoding performance for all task variables combined is significantly higher than for any individual variable, suggesting the variables capture distinct information about neural activity.
papers.limitation:
Relies exclusively on trial-aligned data for pretraining and evaluation, limiting the amount of data available compared to methods using unaligned data.
Due to computational constraints, extensive hyperparameter tuning was not feasible when pretraining on data from all 73 animals.
future_direction: Extend training to incorporate unaligned data to enhance generalizability and leverage larger datasets.
Incorporate additional modalities such as local field potentials and electrophysiological features to enhance cell-type specific functionality prediction.
Utilize standardized benchmarks (e.g., FALCON) for more rigorous and scalable model comparisons.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that large-scale, multi-animal models are powerful tools for characterizing the relationship between neural activity and behavior. Current large-scale approaches, however, focus exclusively on either predicting neural activity from behavior (encoding) or predicting behavior from neural activity (decoding), limiting their ability to capture the bidirectional relationship between neural activity and behavior. To bridge this gap, we introduce a multimodal, multi-task model that enables simultaneous Neural Encoding and Decoding at Scale (NEDS). Central to our approach is a novel multi-task-masking strategy, which alternates between neural, behavioral, within-modality, and cross-modality masking. We pretrain our method on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) repeated site dataset, which includes recordings from 83 animals performing the same visual decision-making task. In comparison to other large-scale models, we demonstrate that NEDS achieves state-of-the-art performance for both encoding and decoding when pretrained on multi-animal data and then fine-tuned on new animals. Surprisingly, NEDS's learned embeddings exhibit emergent properties: even without explicit training, they are highly predictive of the brain regions in each recording. Altogether, our approach is a step towards a foundation model of the brain that enables seamless translation between neural activity and behavior.

papers.title: Representations in vision and language converge in a shared, multidimensional space of perceived similarities
papers.research_question: Do vision and language share a common representational format, and is this format captured by large language model (LLM) embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that human similarity judgments for images and sentences converge on a shared, modality-agnostic representational structure, which predicts brain activity in visual cortex and is best captured by LLM-based computational models.
papers.conclusion: The findings support a shared relational space for vision and language that captures behaviorally relevant structure across sensory modalities and is well modeled by LLM-based systems.
papers.key_findings:
Visual and linguistic similarity judgments are strongly correlated (Spearman ⍴ = 0.781).
Both visual and linguistic similarity judgments predict brain activity in mid- and high-level visual regions.
LLM-trained recurrent convolutional neural networks (RCNNs) better capture the behavioral similarity structure than category-trained RCNNs or AlexNet.
The shared representational structure is grounded in relational properties of the world and is not dependent on first-order visual experience.
The alignment between linguistic judgments and brain activity persists even when participants have not seen the corresponding images.
papers.limitation: The study does not test how behavioral representational geometries align with neural activity during sentence reading.
future_direction: Future research should address the distinct representational dimensions projected from each modality to form a richer representation.
Future research should investigate whether this relational similarity structure is a universal principle extending to other domains like sound or motion perception.
Future fMRI studies of sentence reading are needed to see if similarity judgments predict activity patterns in visual regions during reading.
papers.abstract: Humans can effortlessly describe what they see, yet establishing a shared representational format between vision and language remains a significant challenge. Emerging evidence suggests that human brain representations in both vision and language are well predicted by semantic feature spaces obtained from large language models (LLMs). This raises the possibility that sensory systems converge in their inherent ability to transform their inputs onto shared, embedding-like representational space. However, it remains unclear how such a space manifests in human behaviour. To investigate this, sixty-three participants performed behavioural similarity judgements separately on 100 natural scene images and 100 corresponding sentence captions from the Natural Scenes Dataset. We found that visual and linguistic similarity judgements not only converge at the behavioural level but also predict a remarkably similar network of fMRI brain responses evoked by viewing the natural scene images. Furthermore, computational models trained to map images onto LLM-embeddings outperformed both category-trained and AlexNet controls in explaining the behavioural similarity structure. These findings demonstrate that human visual and linguistic similarity judgements are grounded in a shared, modality-agnostic representational structure that mirrors how the visual system encodes experience. The convergence between sensory and artificial systems suggests a common capacity of how conceptual representations are formed-not as arbitrary products of first order, modality-specific input, but as structured representations that reflect the stable, relational properties of the external world.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: How Vision Becomes Language: A Layer-wise Information-Theoretic Analysis of Multimodal Reasoning
papers.research_question: When a multimodal Transformer answers a visual question, is the prediction driven by visual evidence, linguistic reasoning, or genuinely fused cross-modal computation—and how does this structure evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a layer-wise Partial Information Decomposition (PID) framework and PID Flow estimator, revealing a consistent 'modal transduction' pattern in multimodal Transformers where visual evidence is transformed into language representations early, and late layers are dominated by language-unique information.
papers.conclusion: Current multimodal large language models do not perform emergent cross-modal fusion but rather translate visual evidence into language-space representations for downstream reasoning; PID trajectories offer quantitative guidance for identifying architectural bottlenecks.
papers.key_findings:
Visual-unique information peaks in early layers and decays with depth, while language-unique information surges in late layers, accounting for ~82% of the final prediction; synergy remains low (<2%).
The modal transduction pattern is highly consistent across model variants (LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-1.6) and across six diverse GQA reasoning tasks.
Attention knockout experiments causally validate the transduction pattern: blocking the Image→Question pathway traps visual information, increases synergy, and raises total information cost.
Task semantics modulate the information fingerprint (e.g., redundancy levels) but do not alter the overarching transduction mechanism.
The stage transitions (e.g., onset of language-unique surge) are depth-anchored and stable across models, indicating an architecture-robust mechanism.
papers.abstract: When a multimodal Transformer answers a visual question, is the prediction driven by visual evidence, linguistic reasoning, or genuinely fused cross-modal computation -- and how does this structure evolve across layers? We address this question with a layer-wise framework based on Partial Information Decomposition (PID) that decomposes the predictive information at each Transformer layer into redundant, vision-unique, language-unique, and synergistic components. To make PID tractable for high-dimensional neural representations, we introduce \emph{PID Flow}, a pipeline combining dimensionality reduction, normalizing-flow Gaussianization, and closed-form Gaussian PID estimation. Applying this framework to LLaVA-1.5-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B across six GQA reasoning tasks, we uncover a consistent \emph{modal transduction} pattern: visual-unique information peaks early and decays with depth, language-unique information surges in late layers to account for roughly 82\% of the final prediction, and cross-modal synergy remains below 2\%. This trajectory is highly stable across model variants (layer-wise correlations $>$0.96) yet strongly task-dependent, with semantic redundancy governing the detailed information fingerprint. To establish causality, we perform targeted Image$\rightarrow$Question attention knockouts and show that disrupting the primary transduction pathway induces predictable increases in trapped visual-unique information, compensatory synergy, and total information cost -- effects that are strongest in vision-dependent tasks and weakest in high-redundancy tasks. Together, these results provide an information-theoretic, causal account of how vision becomes language in multimodal Transformers, and offer quantitative guidance for identifying architectural bottlenecks where modality-specific information is lost.

papers.title: The Tensor Brain: Semantic Decoding for Perception and Memory
papers.research_question: How can perception and memory be modeled using tensor models and knowledge graphs, and what insights does this provide into the human mind?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a tensor-based mathematical model for perception and memory, proposing a four-layer complex semantic decoder (sensory memory, representation, index, and working memory) that integrates sensory input with semantic and episodic memory to generate explicit triple statements.
papers.conclusion: The tensor brain model offers a comprehensive mathematical framework for understanding perception and memory, connecting to established cognitive theories and demonstrating strong experimental results on visual relationship benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed tensor model with a four-layer semantic decoder provides a unified framework for perception and memory, linking to cognitive theories like global workspace and Bayesian brain.
The complex semantic decoder, which includes working memory, significantly improves performance on visual relationship detection tasks compared to simpler decoders.
The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets (Visual Genome and VRD) for visual relationship detection.
Semantic memory acts as a prior distribution for triple statements, complementing sensory input and improving decoding accuracy.
The model suggests that explicit perception and declarative memory require working memory and may be unique to humans, enabling complex language and reasoning.
future_direction: Integration of language production capabilities into the model.
Extension to more complex reasoning and planning tasks.
Incorporation of more complex neural architectures and larger-scale datasets.
papers.abstract: We analyse perception and memory, using mathematical models for knowledge graphs and tensors, to gain insights into the corresponding functionalities of the human mind. Our discussion is based on the concept of propositional sentences consisting of \textit{subject-predicate-object} (SPO) triples for expressing elementary facts. SPO sentences are the basis for most natural languages but might also be important for explicit perception and declarative memories, as well as intra-brain communication and the ability to argue and reason. A set of SPO sentences can be described as a knowledge graph, which can be transformed into an adjacency tensor. We introduce tensor models, where concepts have dual representations as indices and associated embeddings, two constructs we believe are essential for the understanding of implicit and explicit perception and memory in the brain. We argue that a biological realization of perception and memory imposes constraints on information processing. In particular, we propose that explicit perception and declarative memories require a semantic decoder, which, in a simple realization, is based on four layers: First, a sensory memory layer, as a buffer for sensory input, second, an index layer representing concepts, third, a memoryless representation layer for the broadcasting of information ---the "blackboard", or the "canvas" of the brain--- and fourth, a working memory layer as a processing center and data buffer. We discuss the operations of the four layers and relate them to the global workspace theory. In a Bayesian brain interpretation, semantic memory defines the prior for observable triple statements. We propose that ---in evolution and during development--- semantic memory, episodic memory, and natural language evolved as emergent properties in agents' process to gain a deeper understanding of sensory information.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: How Do Vision-Language Models Process Conflicting Information Across Modalities?
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models process conflicting information across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that vision-language models exhibit biases towards one modality when processing conflicting inputs, and identifies specific attention heads that can be intervened to improve performance and control the modality preference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs encounter difficulties with conflicting inputs, and their behavioral accuracy correlates with the representational salience of the target modality. Attention head interventions can manipulate the representational salience and improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models show performance degradation when presented with inconsistent image-caption pairs, and different models have different modality biases.
Internal representations encode unimodal information for both modalities and can detect consistency, but the target modality is not always more salient.
The representational salience of the target modality (measured by V-Measure) strongly correlates with behavioral accuracy.
The authors identify modality-agnostic router heads and modality-specific promotion heads through attention head interventions.
Intervening on these heads can improve performance and change representational salience across datasets.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on 7b-parameter multimodal large language models, which are only a subset of vision-language models.
future_direction: Extend findings to inputs from modalities beyond text and vision (e.g., audio, spatial).
Explore circuit analysis to understand interactions among attention heads and other components.
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly required to be multimodal, integrating disparate input streams into a coherent state representation on which subsequent behaviors and actions can be based. This paper seeks to understand how such models behave when input streams present conflicting information. Focusing specifically on vision-language models, we provide inconsistent inputs (e.g., an image of a dog paired with the caption "A photo of a cat") and ask the model to report the information present in one of the specific modalities (e.g., "What does the caption say / What is in the image?"). We find that models often favor one modality over the other, e.g., reporting the image regardless of what the caption says, but that different models differ in which modality they favor. We find evidence that the behaviorally preferred modality is evident in the internal representational structure of the model, and that specific attention heads can restructure the representations to favor one modality over the other. Moreover, we find modality-agnostic "router heads" which appear to promote answers about the modality requested in the instruction, and which can be manipulated or transferred in order to improve performance across datasets and modalities. Together, the work provides essential steps towards identifying and controlling if and how models detect and resolve conflicting signals within complex multimodal environments.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Distillation Dynamics: Towards Understanding Feature-Based Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-based knowledge distillation, which works well for CNNs, fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), and what is the root cause of negative transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern (compression followed by expansion) and identifies a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models as the root cause of negative transfer in feature-based distillation, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViT compression strategies.
papers.conclusion: Successful knowledge transfer in Vision Transformers requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect the fundamental representational constraints and the U-shaped information processing dynamics of these architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models exhibit a learned U-shaped pattern in information entropy and activation magnitude across layers, indicating an initial compression phase followed by a task-specific expansion phase.
The failure of feature-based distillation in ViTs stems from a representational mismatch: teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity.
Late-layer feature alignment actively harms student performance (negative transfer) because it forces the student to adopt a representational paradigm incompatible with its capacity, disrupting its natural learning progression.
Frequency spectrum analysis shows teacher ViTs transition from low-pass to uniform, high-energy spectra in late layers, while CNNs maintain low-pass spectra, explaining why feature mimicry works for CNNs but fails for ViTs.
The U-shaped information processing signature is a consistent learned behavior across different ViT architectures (e.g., CaiT, standard ViT) and training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised like MAE).
papers.abstract: While feature-based knowledge distillation has proven highly effective for compressing CNNs, these techniques unexpectedly fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), often performing worse than simple logit-based distillation. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon through a novel analytical framework termed as "distillation dynamics", combining frequency spectrum analysis, information entropy metrics, and activation magnitude tracking. Our investigation reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern: initial compression followed by expansion. We identify the root cause of negative transfer in feature distillation: a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models. Through frequency-domain analysis, we show that teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding strategies in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity. This mismatch causes late-layer feature alignment to actively harm student performance. Our findings reveal that successful knowledge transfer in ViTs requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect these fundamental representational constraints, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViTs compression strategies. All source code and experimental logs are provided at https://github.com/thy960112/Distillation-Dynamics.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Image denoising with multi-layer perceptrons, part 2: training trade-offs and analysis of their mechanisms
papers.research_question: What trade-offs must be considered when training multi-layer perceptrons for image denoising, and how do these networks internally achieve denoising?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides detailed guidelines for training MLPs to achieve state-of-the-art image denoising and analyzes their inner workings, showing that denoising is achieved through saturation of the tanh activation function, leading to binary hidden representations.
papers.conclusion: MLPs can achieve excellent image denoising performance when trained with appropriate trade-offs, and their internal mechanisms can be understood through analysis of hidden unit activation patterns, revealing a denoising process based on saturation and binary codes.
papers.key_findings:
More training data and more hidden units per layer consistently improve performance.
There exists an ideal number of hidden layers; too many layers, especially in deep and narrow networks, can cause catastrophic performance degradation.
Fine-tuning with a lower learning rate after initial training reduces test error fluctuations and improves final performance.
Denoising in single-hidden-layer MLPs is achieved through saturation of the tanh layer, which attenuates noise while preserving features detected by highly active neurons.
The feature detectors (input weights) adapt to the noise type and strength; for example, larger input patches are learned for stronger noise.
papers.limitation:
Deep and narrow networks (with many hidden layers but few units per layer) are difficult to optimize and can suffer catastrophic degradation in performance.
Block-matching MLPs do not provide a clear advantage at very low or very high noise levels, and their performance can deteriorate compared to plain MLPs at high noise levels.
future_direction: Applying similar training guidelines and analysis to other image processing tasks like super-resolution, deconvolution, and demosaicking.
Exploring the benefits of binary representations compared to sparse representations in deep networks.
papers.abstract: Image denoising can be described as the problem of mapping from a noisy image to a noise-free image. In another paper, we show that multi-layer perceptrons can achieve outstanding image denoising performance for various types of noise (additive white Gaussian noise, mixed Poisson-Gaussian noise, JPEG artifacts, salt-and-pepper noise and noise resembling stripes). In this work we discuss in detail which trade-offs have to be considered during the training procedure. We will show how to achieve good results and which pitfalls to avoid. By analysing the activation patterns of the hidden units we are able to make observations regarding the functioning principle of multi-layer perceptrons trained for image denoising.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Understanding Unimodal Bias in Multimodal Deep Linear Networks
papers.research_question: How do network architecture (fusion depth) and dataset statistics influence unimodal bias in multimodal deep linear networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of unimodal bias in multimodal deep linear networks, showing that deeper fusion layers lead to longer unimodal phases, which can cause generalization deficits and permanent unimodal bias in overparameterized regimes.
papers.conclusion: This work illuminates pathologies of multimodal learning under joint training, showing that late and intermediate fusion architectures can give rise to long unimodal phases and permanent unimodal bias.
papers.key_findings:
Unimodal bias is conspicuous in late and intermediate fusion linear networks but not in early fusion linear networks.
The duration of the unimodal phase depends on fusion depth, dataset statistics (correlations between modalities, input-output correlations), and initialization scale.
Deeper fusion layers lead to longer unimodal phases.
Stronger correlations between input modalities and greater disparities in input-output correlations for each modality prolong the unimodal phase.
In the overparameterized regime, long unimodal phases lead to a generalization deficit and permanent unimodal bias.
papers.limitation: The theory is derived for multimodal linear networks and extends to nonlinear networks only in certain settings.
papers.abstract: Using multiple input streams simultaneously to train multimodal neural networks is intuitively advantageous but practically challenging. A key challenge is unimodal bias, where a network overly relies on one modality and ignores others during joint training. We develop a theory of unimodal bias with multimodal deep linear networks to understand how architecture and data statistics influence this bias. This is the first work to calculate the duration of the unimodal phase in learning as a function of the depth at which modalities are fused within the network, dataset statistics, and initialization. We show that the deeper the layer at which fusion occurs, the longer the unimodal phase. A long unimodal phase can lead to a generalization deficit and permanent unimodal bias in the overparametrized regime. Our results, derived for multimodal linear networks, extend to nonlinear networks in certain settings. Taken together, this work illuminates pathologies of multimodal learning under joint training, showing that late and intermediate fusion architectures can give rise to long unimodal phases and permanent unimodal bias. Our code is available at: https://yedizhang.github.io/unimodal-bias.html.

papers.title: Escaping Plato's Cave: JAM for Aligning Independently Trained Vision and Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we move beyond post-hoc detection of alignment between independently trained vision and language models and explicitly optimize for it, particularly in fine-grained contextual distinctions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM) and a novel multimodal Spread Loss to align frozen, independently trained vision and language models, demonstrating that post-hoc alignment can rival or outperform generalist multimodal models in fine-grained specialist tasks.
papers.conclusion: Independently trained unimodal representations can be aligned post hoc via lightweight autoencoders and structured supervision (Spread loss), revealing a shared Platonic representation and offering a practical recipe for building specialist multimodal models from frozen unimodal foundations.
papers.key_findings:
JAM with Spread loss consistently outperforms contrastive baselines and pretrained/finetuned CLIP on fine-grained vision-language compositionality tasks.
The reconstruction component in JAM acts as a critical regularizer; removing it leads to overfitting and performance drop.
Optimal alignment supervision varies with layer depth: earlier layers require stronger fine-grained contrastive pressure (higher α in Spread loss).
Scaling up the language backbone does not consistently improve alignment performance in fine-grained tasks, suggesting task-specific alignment is more important than model scale.
Statistical tests (CKA, CCA, etc.) show independently trained models have coarse-grained alignment but fail to capture fine-grained distinctions.
future_direction: Extending to domains requiring highly specific reasoning (e.g., legal, medical, scientific).
Scaling to larger datasets and models.
Exploring more sophisticated alignment approaches beyond Spread loss.
Studying alignment for more than two modalities simultaneously (e.g., time series).
papers.abstract: Independently trained vision and language models inhabit disjoint representational spaces, shaped by their respective modalities, objectives, and architectures. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests these models may nonetheless converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. This raises a fundamental question: can we move beyond post-hoc detection of such alignment and explicitly optimize for it? We argue this challenge is most critical in fine-grained contextual distinctions-where multiple descriptions share global semantics but differ in subtle compositional details. We address this with the Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM), which aligns frozen unimodal models by jointly training modality-specific autoencoders with coordinated reconstruction and cross-modal alignment objectives. We systematically evaluate JAM across three design axes: (i) alignment objectives, introducing our multimodal Spread Loss that outperforms classic contrastive methods; (ii) the layer depth at which alignment is most effective; and (iii) the role of foundation model scale in representational convergence. Our findings show that JAM reliably induces alignment even across independently trained representations, offering both theoretical insight into the structure of shared semantics and practical guidance for transforming generalist unimodal foundations into specialist multimodal models.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation; the token identity then gets recreated at the top layer.
For MT, though representations get refined with context, less processing is happening and most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
Frequent tokens change more than rare ones in all layers for LM and MT, but for MLM the pattern is different with two stages; rare tokens generally influence more than frequent ones, except in MLM where the model learns not to over-rely on rare tokens before context is understood.
papers.limitation: Direct mutual information estimation from finite samples for densities on multi-dimensional spaces is challenging.
papers.abstract: We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
papers.research_question: How can we automatically explain features in image representations using natural language concepts? Also, which features in the representation space are explainable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces FALCON, an automatic framework for explaining image representation features using natural language concepts. It also shows that interpretable subspaces are often composed of feature groups rather than individual features.
papers.conclusion: FALCON provides an effective way to automatically explain features in image representations. The study reveals that interpretable subspaces often consist of feature groups, and the extracted concepts can be used for debugging and transfer.
papers.key_findings:
FALCON can automatically extract human-understandable concepts for features without human intervention.
Individual features are often not interpretable, but groups of features are more interpretable.
FALCON concepts are validated by human evaluation with high precision and recall.
Concepts can be used to explain failures in downstream tasks.
Concepts can be transferred across representation spaces via a linear transformation.
papers.limitation:
The quality of explanations is dependent on the captioning dataset and the vision-language model.
The method may not capture very high-level abstract concepts that are not well-represented in the captioning data.
future_direction: Extending FALCON to other modalities like text and audio.
Improving the concept extraction to handle more abstract features.
Exploring the use of FALCON for model editing and improving model robustness.
papers.abstract: We propose Automatic Feature Explanation using Contrasting Concepts (FALCON), an interpretability framework to explain features of image representations. For a target feature, FALCON captions its highly activating cropped images using a large captioning dataset (like LAION-400m) and a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP. Each word among the captions is scored and ranked leading to a small number of shared, human-understandable concepts that closely describe the target feature. FALCON also applies contrastive interpretation using lowly activating (counterfactual) images, to eliminate spurious concepts. Although many existing approaches interpret features independently, we observe in state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised models, that less than 20% of the representation space can be explained by individual features. We show that features in larger spaces become more interpretable when studied in groups and can be explained with high-order scoring concepts through FALCON. We discuss how extracted concepts can be used to explain and debug failures in downstream tasks. Finally, we present a technique to transfer concepts from one (explainable) representation space to another unseen representation space by learning a simple linear transformation. Code available at https://github.com/NehaKalibhat/falcon-explain.

papers.title: Metric Learning Encoding Models: A Multivariate Framework for Interpreting Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural representations by learning a metric over theoretical features that matches the geometry of the neural space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Metric Learning Encoding Models (MLEMs), a multivariate encoding framework that learns a metric over theoretical features to match the geometry of neural representations, enabling modeling of feature interactions and robust feature importance estimation.
papers.conclusion: MLEM provides a versatile and robust tool for interpreting high-dimensional neural representations by modeling the geometry of the feature space to match the neural geometry, applicable across modalities in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
MLEM recovers ground-truth feature weights more accurately than the FR-RSA-I baseline in synthetic simulations.
MLEM is more robust to noise in neural representations compared to FR-RSA-I.
MLEM converges faster during training than FR-RSA-I.
MLEM identifies similar feature importance profiles as FR-RSA-I on real language data but with greater stability.
The symmetric positive definite constraint on the weight matrix provides regularization, leading to improved accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
For very large and heterogeneous datasets, the subsampling strategy may miss informative stimulus pairs related to sparse features, potentially biasing the learned metric.
The framework does not weight individual neural units, which could improve alignment but at the cost of interpretability.
future_direction: Applying MLEM to human brain data (fMRI, MEG, ECoG) to bridge computational models and biological neural computation.
Using MLEM to interpret internal representations of deep learning models across various modalities.
Leveraging MLEM's ability to uncover hierarchical clustering for discovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional representations.
papers.abstract: Understanding how explicit theoretical features are encoded in opaque neural systems is a central challenge now common to neuroscience and AI. We introduce Metric Learning Encoding Models (MLEMs) to address this challenge most directly as a metric learning problem: we fit the distance in the space of theoretical features to match the distance in neural space. Our framework improves on univariate encoding and decoding methods by building on second-order isomorphism methods, such as Representational Similarity Analysis, and extends them by learning a metric that efficiently models feature as well as interactions between them. The effectiveness of MLEM is validated through two sets of simulations. First, MLEMs recover ground-truth importance features in synthetic datasets better than state-of-the-art methods, such as Feature Reweighted RSA (FR-RSA). Second, we deploy MLEMs on real language data, where they show stronger robustness to noise in calculating the importance of linguistic features (gender, tense, etc.). MLEMs are applicable to any domains where theoretical features can be identified, such as language, vision, audition, etc. We release optimized code applicable to measure feature importance in the representations of any artificial neural networks or empirical neural data at https://github.com/LouisJalouzot/MLEM.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings.
