We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
papers.research_question: How are linguistic features encoded in the linear geometry of contextualized word representations, and what are the geometric properties of these encodings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional linear subspaces of contextualized word representations, that these subspaces have hierarchical structure and are distributed across neurons, and that they are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a probing procedure that reveals low-dimensional linear subspaces encoding linguistic features in word representations, with hierarchical and distributed structure, and shows these subspaces are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces of contextualized word representations.
These subspaces exhibit hierarchical structure (e.g., noun and verb subspaces nested within part-of-speech subspaces).
The subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than aligned with individual axes.
Ablating specific subspaces (e.g., nounspace or verbspace) impairs BERT's performance on subject-verb agreement, indicating causal relevance.
Contextual representations encode linguistic variables better but not more compactly than non-contextual word embeddings.
future_direction: Explore richer geometric structure in word representations and its effect on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that lowdimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT's output distribution.

papers.title: Towards a Unified Representation Evaluation Framework Beyond Downstream Tasks
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate model representations beyond downstream tasks by quantifying attributes like informativeness, equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework to evaluate model representations along axes of informativeness, equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement, showing that models with similar downstream performance can have different structural properties.
papers.conclusion: Introduces a standardized framework for representation evaluation beyond downstream tasks, emphasizing the importance of structural properties for understanding model behavior and encouraging future extensions.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar downstream performance exhibit different behaviors in equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement.
Informativeness and equivariance are not always correlated; for example, contrastive models may show strong invariance but poor equivariance.
Scale impacts performance inconsistently across axes, with larger models sometimes encoding factors less accessibly.
Disentanglement is model-dependent and non-bijective, meaning disentanglement from one factor to another does not guarantee the reverse.
The framework reveals structural differences in representations that are not captured by downstream probing alone.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a restricted set of factors, metrics, and axes, using only parametric transformations with clear factor correspondences.
future_direction: Explore more complex factors of variation, including non-parametric transformations and higher-level semantic shifts.
Extend the framework with new metrics and apply it to broader domains.
papers.abstract: Downstream probing has been the dominant method for evaluating model representations, an important process given the increasing prominence of self-supervised learning and foundation models. However, downstream probing primarily assesses the availability of task-relevant information in the model's latent space, overlooking attributes such as equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement, which contribute to the interpretability, adaptability, and utility of representations in real-world applications. While some attempts have been made to measure these qualities in representations, no unified evaluation framework with modular, generalizable, and interpretable metrics exists. In this paper, we argue for the importance of representation evaluation beyond downstream probing. We introduce a standardized protocol to quantify informativeness, equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement of factors of variation in model representations. We use it to evaluate representations from a variety of models in the image and speech domains using different architectures and pretraining approaches on identified controllable factors of variation. We find that representations from models with similar downstream performance can behave substantially differently with regard to these attributes. This hints that the respective mechanisms underlying their downstream performance are functionally different, prompting new research directions to understand and improve representations.

papers.title: How to Teach DNNs to Pay Attention to the Visual Modality in Speech Recognition
papers.research_question: How does the AV Align method for audio-visual speech recognition work internally, and how can it be improved to better exploit the visual modality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a regularization method using an auxiliary loss for predicting lip-related Action Units, which helps the AV Align architecture learn better visual representations and significantly improves audio-visual speech recognition performance, especially in noisy conditions.
papers.conclusion: AV Align is the first architecture to explicitly learn asynchronous alignments between audio and visual speech modalities, and the proposed Action Unit regularization simplifies training and leads to significant performance gains in audio-visual speech recognition.
papers.key_findings:
AV Align learns to align acoustic and visual speech representations at the frame level in a generally monotonic pattern.
Without regularization, the visual front-end in AV Align can fail to converge, leading to no improvement over audio-only recognition on challenging datasets like LRS2.
Adding an auxiliary loss for predicting lip-related Action Units (AU25 and AU26) regularizes the visual front-end, enabling performance improvements of 7% to 30% depending on noise level.
The proposed Action Unit loss also helps the Watch, Listen, Attend, and Spell (WLAS) network learn visual representations and improve performance.
The cross-modal alignment patterns learned by AV Align are interpretable and show phonetic correlations, such as varying asynchronies between audio and video related to plosive sounds.
papers.limitation: The audio-visual system does not always fall back to audio-only performance when the visual modality is not informative, which can lead to errors in some sentences.
future_direction: Future AVSR systems should be designed to assess confidence in the visual content and fall back to audio-only performance when the visual modality is unreliable.
A deeper analysis of the learnt audio-visual alignments and their phonetic implications is left as future work.
papers.abstract: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) seeks to model, and thereby exploit, the dynamic relationship between a human voice and the corresponding mouth movements. A recently proposed multimodal fusion strategy, AV Align, based on state-of-the-art sequence to sequence neural networks, attempts to model this relationship by explicitly aligning the acoustic and visual representations of speech. This study investigates the inner workings of AV Align and visualises the audio-visual alignment patterns. Our experiments are performed on two of the largest publicly available AVSR datasets, TCD-TIMIT and LRS2. We find that AV Align learns to align acoustic and visual representations of speech at the frame level on TCD-TIMIT in a generally monotonic pattern. We also determine the cause of initially seeing no improvement over audio-only speech recognition on the more challenging LRS2. We propose a regularisation method which involves predicting lip-related Action Units from visual representations. Our regularisation method leads to better exploitation of the visual modality, with performance improvements between 7% and 30% depending on the noise level. Furthermore, we show that the alternative Watch, Listen, Attend, and Spell network is affected by the same problem as AV Align, and that our proposed approach can effectively help it learn visual representations. Our findings validate the suitability of the regularisation method to AVSR and encourage researchers to rethink the multimodal convergence problem when having one dominant modality.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.research_question: Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes.
papers.core_contribution: LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by natural scenes and provide a representational format that accounts for complex visual information extracted by the brain.
papers.conclusion: LLM embeddings provide a versatile representational format for capturing complex information derived by the brain from visual inputs, paving the way for new research avenues.
papers.key_findings:
LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully predict brain activity across higher-level visual areas.
Linear encoding and decoding models using LLM embeddings can capture region-specific tuning properties and reconstruct accurate scene captions from brain activity.
The alignment derives from LLMs' ability to integrate complex information beyond individual words or object categories.
ANNs trained to predict LLM embeddings from images learn representations better aligned with brain activity than many state-of-the-art models, despite less training data.
papers.limitation: The task of the NSD participants was to report if they had previously seen each presented image. It cannot be fully ruled out that, to perform this continuous recognition task, participants were internally captioning the scenes, and this may have benefitted the LLM caption embeddings as a good model of visual responses.
future_direction: Exploring datasets where prepositions, adjectives and adverbs play a more important role is an intriguing direction for future research.
An interesting future direction of research will spell out whether the rich learning signal derived from language might indeed provide important benefits over other training objectives.
It will be interesting for future work to investigate LLM-based codes under different tasks.
papers.abstract: The human brain extracts complex information from visual inputs, including objects, their spatial and semantic interrelations, and their interactions with the environment. However, a quantitative approach for studying this information remains elusive. Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes. We show that LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by viewing the natural scenes. This mapping captures selectivities of different brain areas and is sufficiently robust that accurate scene captions can be reconstructed from brain activity. Using carefully controlled model comparisons, we then proceed to show that the accuracy with which LLM representations match brain representations derives from the ability of LLMs to integrate complex information contained in scene captions beyond that conveyed by individual words. Finally, we train deep neural network models to transform image inputs into LLM representations. Remarkably, these networks learn representations that are better aligned with brain representations than a large number of state-of-the-art alternative models, despite being trained on orders-of-magnitude less data. Overall, our results suggest that LLM embeddings of scene captions provide a representational format that accounts for complex information extracted by the brain from visual inputs.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Late Fusion and Multi-Level Fission Amplify Cross-Modal Transfer in Text-Speech LMs
papers.research_question: How should a model originally designed to process and generate text adapt to handle non-textual modalities (specifically speech) so as to promote cross-modal knowledge transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an architecture for text-speech language models featuring late fusion, multi-level fission, and late fission, which significantly improves cross-modal transfer and performance compared to early fusion/fission baselines.
papers.conclusion: Late fusion/fission and multi-level fission architectures that respect the compositional hierarchy of multimodal features are key to efficiently adapting text LMs to other perceptual modalities, as demonstrated by the superior performance of SMOLTOLK models.
papers.key_findings:
SMOLTOLK models outperform early fusion/fission baselines across all evaluated tasks and scale more efficiently with compute.
The proposed architecture enhances the model's ability to abstract higher-level, more semantic features from speech and leads to increasingly shared representation spaces across layers.
Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component (late fusion, multi-level fission, late fission, residual connection) contributes to improved performance.
SMOLTOLK-2B rivals or surpasses state-of-the-art TSLMs trained with orders of magnitude more compute.
The method exhibits less deterioration in text capabilities (MMLU) after speech training compared to prior work.
papers.limitation:
Models are small by current standards, and observed phenomena may differ at larger scales.
The model is not instruction fine-tuned, limiting direct applicability to tasks like spoken conversational agents.
Using HuBERT-based tokens limits expressivity compared to more expressive speech representations.
future_direction: Explore instruction tuning and broader evaluations for practical applications.
Apply the architecture to model more expressive speech representations.
papers.abstract: Text-Speech Language Models (TSLMs) -- language models trained to jointly process and generate text and speech -- are commonly trained through an early modality fusion/fission approach, in which both modalities are fed and predicted from a shared backbone via linear layers. We hypothesize that this approach limits cross-modal transfer by neglecting feature compositionality -- specifically, the finer-grained nature of speech representations compared to text -- preventing the emergence of a shared feature hierarchy within model layers. In this paper, we argue that this limitation can be addressed through late fusion and fission, with a fission process that accesses both high- and low-level features for speech generation. Our models implementing these principles, SmolTolk, rival or surpass state-of-the-art TSLMs trained with orders of magnitude more compute, and achieve significantly improved cross-modal performance relative to early fusion/fission baselines. Representation analyses further suggest that our method enhances the model's ability to abstract higher-level, more semantic features from speech, and leads to increasingly shared representation spaces across layers.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring the activation boundaries of hidden neurons, rather than the magnitude of their responses, improve the performance of knowledge transfer between neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills the activation boundaries (separating hyperplanes determining neuron activation) from a teacher network to a student network, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: Transferring activation boundaries is a powerful approach for knowledge transfer, leading to superior performance in terms of learning speed, generalization with limited data, and network compression, and can potentially replace pre-training in some scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed activation boundary transfer method accelerates student network training more effectively than existing methods.
The method significantly improves student network generalization when training data is limited.
The method is effective for various network compression scenarios (depth, channel, and combined compression).
In transfer learning tasks, the method can outperform training a student network with ImageNet pre-training.
The proposed alternative loss function successfully approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high neuron activation similarity between teacher and student.
future_direction: Modifying various tasks that rely on pre-training to accommodate knowledge transfer for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classification friendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Under the Hood of Neural Networks: Characterizing Learned Representations by Functional Neuron Populations and Network Ablations
papers.research_question: What are the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within a neural network in fulfilling a learned task? How can learned representations be characterized by activation patterns and network ablations to reveal functional neuron populations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper characterizes learned representations in neural networks by identifying functional neuron populations through activation patterns and network ablations, showing that a neuron's activation magnitude, selectivity, and impact on performance are insufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how knowledge is represented and localized in artificial networks is beneficial for advancing transfer learning and for providing measures for large-scale studies in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Learned representations evolve to become more distinct along network layers, improving class separation in the activation-space.
Network ablations distort the activation-space, leading to misclassifications, but the relative positions of units are mostly preserved, suggesting a holistic effect.
Functional neuron populations exist: groups of neurons that jointly activate in response to specific stimuli or have a similar impact on network accuracy when ablated.
The size of functional neuron populations varies greatly across classes, indicating different network capacity usage per class.
No single metric (activation magnitude, selectivity, or ablation impact) sufficiently describes the role of a single unit within the whole network.
papers.limitation:
The number of samples (10 classes) is small, limiting the descriptive statistical power of the correlation tests.
Investigating the effect of single unit ablations does not allow determining whether the ablated unit is singly important or part of an important path through the network that has been altered.
future_direction: Determine how robustness of class-specific representations against network ablations can be characterized and achieved purposefully.
Identify important paths along the network, rather than just single units, to understand the flow of information.
Investigate how the localization of a class-specific representation is affected by class-specific properties and how the robustness of these representations depends on these properties.
papers.abstract: The need for more transparency of the decision-making processes in artificial neural networks steadily increases driven by their applications in safety critical and ethically challenging domains such as autonomous driving or medical diagnostics. We address today's lack of transparency of neural networks and shed light on the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within the network fulfilling a learned task. Inspired by research in the field of neuroscience, we characterize the learned representations by activation patterns and network ablations, revealing functional neuron populations that a) act jointly in response to specific stimuli or b) have similar impact on the network's performance after being ablated. We find that neither a neuron's magnitude or selectivity of activation, nor its impact on network performance are sufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance for the overall task. We argue that such indicators are essential for future advances in transfer learning and modern neuroscience.

papers.title: SHARCS: Shared Concept Space for Explainable Multimodal Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design an explainable multimodal learning approach that learns interpretable concepts from different modalities and maps them into a unified shared concept space to improve predictive performance and provide cross-modal explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SHARCS, a concept-based approach for explainable multimodal learning that maps interpretable concepts from different heterogeneous modalities into a unified shared concept space, leading to improved predictive performance and cross-modal explanations.
papers.conclusion: SHARCS provides an explainable multimodal learning approach that improves performance and offers valuable insights into cross-modal relationships, advancing the development of effective, interpretable, and trustworthy multimodal agents.
papers.key_findings:
SHARCS outperforms unimodal models and matches or outperforms multimodal baselines on four tasks.
SHARCS achieves high task accuracy even when a modality is missing.
SHARCS generates intuitive concept-based explanations for task predictions.
SHARCS generates cross-modal explanations, allowing one modality to be explained using another.
SHARCS learns more compact and better concepts, as evidenced by higher completeness scores.
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning is an essential paradigm for addressing complex real-world problems, where individual data modalities are typically insufficient to accurately solve a given modelling task. While various deep learning approaches have successfully addressed these challenges, their reasoning process is often opaque; limiting the capabilities for a principled explainable cross-modal analysis and any domain-expert intervention. In this paper, we introduce SHARCS (SHARed Concept Space) -- a novel concept-based approach for explainable multimodal learning. SHARCS learns and maps interpretable concepts from different heterogeneous modalities into a single unified concept-manifold, which leads to an intuitive projection of semantically similar cross-modal concepts. We demonstrate that such an approach can lead to inherently explainable task predictions while also improving downstream predictive performance. Moreover, we show that SHARCS can operate and significantly outperform other approaches in practically significant scenarios, such as retrieval of missing modalities and cross-modal explanations. Our approach is model-agnostic and easily applicable to different types (and number) of modalities, thus advancing the development of effective, interpretable, and trustworthy multimodal approaches.

papers.title: Local vs distributed representations: What is the right basis for interpretability?
papers.research_question: Are dictionary-based representations more interpretable than neuron-based representations for understanding convolutional neural networks, and how does the choice of representational basis affect model comparisons?
papers.core_contribution: Dictionary-based representations are consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations in CNNs, and model comparisons based solely on neuron-level analyses can be misleading due to differences in superposition.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary-based representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, and comparing models using only neuron-based representations can lead to misleading conclusions about their relative interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations across three psychophysics experiments, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.
ResNet50 exhibits greater superposition (lower axis-alignment) than VGG16, which masks its higher interpretability in neuron-based comparisons.
ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 when evaluated using dictionary-based representations, but this difference disappears when using neuron-based representations.
Dictionary elements are at least as decision-relevant as individual neurons, as measured by Gradient×Input importance.
papers.limitation:
The experimental protocol may be confounded by semantics, as participants could solve trials by simple semantic grouping rather than identifying visual patterns.
The study is limited to two CNN architectures (ResNet50 and VGG16).
future_direction: Further refinement of the experimental protocol to better mitigate semantic confounds.
Examination of the interpretability of dictionary elements recovered by applying dictionary learning to full layer activations.
Expanding the range of architectures to understand why certain models are inherently more interpretable than others.
papers.abstract: Much of the research on the interpretability of deep neural networks has focused on studying the visual features that maximally activate individual neurons. However, recent work has cast doubts on the usefulness of such local representations for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks because individual neurons tend to respond to multiple unrelated visual patterns, a phenomenon referred to as "superposition". A promising alternative to disentangle these complex patterns is learning sparsely distributed vector representations from entire network layers, as the resulting basis vectors seemingly encode single identifiable visual patterns consistently. Thus, one would expect the resulting code to align better with human perceivable visual patterns, but supporting evidence remains, at best, anecdotal. To fill this gap, we conducted three large-scale psychophysics experiments collected from a pool of 560 participants. Our findings provide (i) strong evidence that features obtained from sparse distributed representations are easier to interpret by human observers and (ii) that this effect is more pronounced in the deepest layers of a neural network. Complementary analyses also reveal that (iii) features derived from sparse distributed representations contribute more to the model's decision. Overall, our results highlight that distributed representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, underscoring a need for the field to move beyond the interpretation of local neural codes in favor of sparsely distributed ones.

papers.title: Deep Sparse Coding for Invariant Multimodal Halle Berry Neurons
papers.research_question: Can augmenting deep neural networks with biologically inspired concepts of sparsity, lateral inhibition, and top-down feedback lead to the emergence of invariant multimodal neurons and improve representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a deep sparse coding model augmented with lateral inhibition and top-down feedback, which leads to the emergence of invariant multimodal neurons (like the 'Halle Berry neuron') and produces more separable feature representations compared to a standard feed-forward autoencoder.
papers.conclusion: Augmenting a standard feed-forward autoencoder with biologically inspired concepts of sparsity, lateral inhibition, and top-down feedback leads to the emergence of invariant multimodal neurons and more separable features, demonstrating the benefits of these concepts.
papers.key_findings:
The DSC model produces invariant neurons that respond to the same concept (e.g., Halle Berry) across different modalities (image and text).
The joint embedding layer in the DSC model has a much higher percentage of multimodal neurons (59.76%) compared to the FFA model (5.27%).
The DSC model produces sparser representations (20.2% sparse) than the FFA model (47.8% sparse) without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
Features extracted from the DSC model are more linearly separable, as visualized by t-SNE plots.
The DSC model can generate missing modalities (e.g., text from image) with similar accuracy to the FFA model but with better reconstruction quality of the input.
papers.limitation:
The model is computationally expensive (slow inference) compared to feed-forward models.
The model has not been tested on many datasets.
future_direction: Experiment with pixels and audio waveforms in the multimodal deep sparse coding model.
Explore invariant representations of audio and text.
papers.abstract: Deep feed-forward convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become ubiquitous in virtually all machine learning and computer vision challenges; however, advancements in CNNs have arguably reached an engineering saturation point where incremental novelty results in minor performance gains. Although there is evidence that object classification has reached human levels on narrowly defined tasks, for general applications, the biological visual system is far superior to that of any computer. Research reveals there are numerous missing components in feed-forward deep neural networks that are critical in mammalian vision. The brain does not work solely in a feed-forward fashion, but rather all of the neurons are in competition with each other; neurons are integrating information in a bottom up and top down fashion and incorporating expectation and feedback in the modeling process. Furthermore, our visual cortex is working in tandem with our parietal lobe, integrating sensory information from various modalities. In our work, we sought to improve upon the standard feed-forward deep learning model by augmenting them with biologically inspired concepts of sparsity, top-down feedback, and lateral inhibition. We define our model as a sparse coding problem using hierarchical layers. We solve the sparse coding problem with an additional top-down feedback error driving the dynamics of the neural network. While building and observing the behavior of our model, we were fascinated that multimodal, invariant neurons naturally emerged that mimicked, "Halle Berry neurons" found in the human brain. Furthermore, our sparse representation of multimodal signals demonstrates qualitative and quantitative superiority to the standard feed-forward joint embedding in common vision and machine learning tasks.

papers.title: Latent Neural Representations Analysis and Distillation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we effectively distill Transformer models when there is a dimensionality mismatch between teacher and student, and how can analysis of latent neural representations (like outlier dimensions) inform better distillation algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two novel distillation methods: Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) for handling mismatched attention heads between teacher and student models, and Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) which prioritizes critical outlier dimensions in latent representations. It also provides the first systematic analysis of emergent outlier dimensions in Encoder-Decoder T5 and instruction-finetuned Flan-T5 models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for analyzing and distilling latent neural representations advance the understanding and acceleration of Transformer inference, with AMAD and EOFD demonstrating state-of-the-art distillation performance and generalization across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
AMAD enables effective distillation between teacher and student Transformers with different numbers of attention heads, outperforming conventional methods on vision-language tasks like VQA and captioning.
Outlier dimensions in T5 and Flan-T5 models, identified by unusually large activation magnitudes, are critical for zero-shot performance and are shared across layers within the encoder or decoder, but differ between encoder and decoder.
EOFD, which focuses distillation loss on these outlier dimensions, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE benchmark and generalizes across BERT, GPT-2, and T5 architectures.
Distillation with AMAD can compensate for the absence of vision-language pre-training, and in some cases, distilled students outperform pre-trained and fine-tuned teachers.
The growth of outlier magnitude in T5 models is more correlated with increasing layer depth rather than overall model size, contrary to findings in GPT models.
papers.limitation: In some cases, a Teacher attention head may not be similar to any Student head after AMAD distillation, indicating a potential failure mode for knowledge transfer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-backed Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models are among the most widely used machine learning models recently. However, due to their enormous size, their behaviors and dynamics become difficult to understand and explain, and their inference speed and cost become slow and forbidding. Therefore, understanding their latent neural patterns and distilling their latent neural representations into smaller, cheaper, and faster models are vital for creating more explainable, accessible, and sustainable machine intelligence. However, knowledge distillation algorithms face an inherent challenge in minimizing the divergence between the neural activation representations of a teacher Transformer and a student Transformer: The latent representation spaces of the smaller Student always have lower dimensionality than those of the larger Teacher. We will address this Transformer distillation dimensionality mismatch or reduction problem by analyzing the neural activation patterns within these latent representation spaces and by proposing corresponding novel algorithms for distilling each group of components of Transformers. Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Representation Convergence: Mutual Distillation is Secretly a Form of Regularization
papers.research_question: What hinders reinforcement learning agents from generalizing like humans? How can we enable them to learn robust representations that drive human-like generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies acts as an implicit regularization by improving policy robustness to irrelevant features, which leads to better generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mutual distillation is a form of implicit regularization that improves generalization in reinforcement learning by enhancing policy robustness to irrelevant features and promoting invariant representations.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, improving policy robustness to irrelevant features enhances generalization performance.
Empirically, mutual distillation (DML) improves generalization performance across Procgen environments.
DML leads to more robust representations that are invariant to irrelevant features, as visualized by t-SNE.
The proposed MDPO algorithm consistently outperforms the PPO baseline in generalization.
Ablation studies indicate the improvement is due to regularization against irrelevant features, not merely additional information sharing.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we argue that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies serves as an implicit regularization, preventing them from overfitting to irrelevant features. We highlight two separate contributions: (i) Theoretically, for the first time, we prove that enhancing the policy robustness to irrelevant features leads to improved generalization performance. (ii) Empirically, we demonstrate that mutual distillation between policies contributes to such robustness, enabling the spontaneous emergence of invariant representations over pixel inputs. Ultimately, we do not claim to achieve state-of-the-art performance but rather focus on uncovering the underlying principles of generalization and deepening our understanding of its mechanisms.

papers.title: Causal Tracing of Object Representations in Large Vision Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability and Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How do large vision-language models process and represent visual object information, and how can we use this understanding to mitigate object hallucination?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce the Fine-grained Cross-modal Causal Tracing (FCCT) framework to analyze how LVLMs process visual object information, and based on the findings, we propose Intermediate Representation Injection (IRI), a training-free inference-time technique that mitigates object hallucination.
papers.conclusion: The FCCT framework provides comprehensive insights into LVLM internal mechanisms, and the IRI technique effectively mitigates object hallucinations in a training-free, model-agnostic manner.
papers.key_findings:
MHSA of the last token in middle layers plays a critical role in aggregating cross-modal information from visual and textual tokens.
FFNs exhibit a three-stage hierarchical progression for the storage and transfer of visual object representations.
Hidden states show a semantic shift from visual-centric in shallow layers to cross-modal and task-related in deep layers.
The proposed IRI method achieves state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation performance across multiple benchmarks and LVLMs.
IRI preserves inference speed and other foundational model capabilities while mitigating hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable advancements of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), the mechanistic interpretability remains underexplored. Existing analyses are insufficiently comprehensive and lack examination covering visual and textual tokens, model components, and the full range of layers. This limitation restricts actionable insights to improve the faithfulness of model output and the development of downstream tasks, such as hallucination mitigation. To address this limitation, we introduce Fine-grained Cross-modal Causal Tracing (FCCT) framework, which systematically quantifies the causal effects on visual object perception. FCCT conducts fine-grained analysis covering the full range of visual and textual tokens, three core model components including multi-head self-attention (MHSA), feed-forward networks (FFNs), and hidden states, across all decoder layers. Our analysis is the first to demonstrate that MHSAs of the last token in middle layers play a critical role in aggregating cross-modal information, while FFNs exhibit a three-stage hierarchical progression for the storage and transfer of visual object representations. Building on these insights, we propose Intermediate Representation Injection (IRI), a training-free inference-time technique that reinforces visual object information flow by precisely intervening on cross-modal representations at specific components and layers, thereby enhancing perception and mitigating hallucination. Consistent improvements across five widely used benchmarks and LVLMs demonstrate IRI achieves state-of-the-art performance, while preserving inference speed and other foundational performance.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: A quantitative analysis of semantic information in deep representations of text and images
papers.research_question: How does semantic information converge across languages, modalities, and architectures in deep representations, and how can we quantify the directed predictability between representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that semantic information in deep representations is spread across many tokens and is strongest in central layers for autoregressive models and final layers for encoder models, with information asymmetries depending on language, model scale, and modality.
papers.conclusion: The results support the hypothesis of semantic convergence across languages, modalities, and architectures, while showing that directed predictability between representations varies strongly with layer-depth, model scale, and language.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic information is spread across many tokens in deep layers, not concentrated in the last token.
For autoregressive models (like DeepSeek-V3), semantic predictability is strongest in central layers, while for encoder models (like DinoV2) it is strongest in the final layers.
Information asymmetries exist: English representations are more predictive of translations than other languages, and larger models (DeepSeek-V3) are more predictive of smaller models (Llama3-8b) than the reverse.
Cross-modal predictability between independently trained large models (DeepSeek-V3 and DinoV2) can be stronger than that of jointly trained multimodal models (CLIP), suggesting model scale may outweigh explicit multimodal training.
The Information Imbalance metric is effective in quantifying directed predictability between representations, outperforming symmetric metrics like CKA and NO in high-dimensional settings.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are known to develop similar representations for semantically related data, even when they belong to different domains, such as an image and its description, or the same text in different languages. We present a method for quantitatively investigating this phenomenon by measuring the relative information content of the representations of semantically related data and probing how it is encoded into multiple tokens of large language models (LLMs) and vision transformers. Looking first at how LLMs process pairs of translated sentences, we identify inner ``semantic'' layers containing the most language-transferable information. We find moreover that, on these layers, a larger LLM (DeepSeek-V3) extracts significantly more general information than a smaller one (Llama3.1-8B). Semantic information of English text is spread across many tokens and it is characterized by long-distance correlations between tokens and by a causal left-to-right (i.e., past-future) asymmetry. We also identify layers encoding semantic information within visual transformers. We show that caption representations in the semantic layers of LLMs predict visual representations of the corresponding images. We observe significant and model-dependent information asymmetries between image and text representations.

papers.title: Semantic Brain Decoding: from fMRI to conceptually similar image reconstruction of visual stimuli
papers.research_question: Can fMRI data from the visual cortex be used to reconstruct images that are semantically similar to the original visual stimuli, by mapping brain activity to the latent space of a convolutional neural network and then generating images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel brain decoding pipeline that linearly maps fMRI data to the latent space of a pretrained CNN (ResNet50), uses a nearest-neighbor strategy to predict semantic categories, and conditions a pretrained latent diffusion model to generate novel images that are semantically similar to the original visual stimuli, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: The study provides evidence that fMRI data can be linearly mapped to the latent space of a CNN to synthesize images conceptually similar to original stimuli, mimicking the combination of bottom-up visual input and top-down cognitive processing in human vision.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed pipeline generates images that are semantically and contextually close to the original visual stimuli, as evidenced by qualitative comparisons and quantitative metrics.
The model achieves a Wu-Palmer similarity of 0.57 on the test set and an 81% correct selection rate in human evaluation, demonstrating good semantic reconstruction.
The approach works well even when training and test image categories do not overlap, suggesting the model captures general semantic features rather than specific class information.
A linear mapping (ridge regression) from fMRI data to CNN latent features is sufficient for effective reconstruction, supporting the hypothesis of a homeomorphic relationship.
The method outperforms previous approaches on the same 3T fMRI dataset, potentially widening applicability to centers without ultra-high-field scanners.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI experiments are restricted in length, limiting the applicability of end-to-end deep learning algorithms.
The model's performance depends on the relationship between fMRI data and image features in the training set, and may degrade if test categories are highly dissimilar and underrepresented in training.
Potential sources of error include fMRI acquisition noise, bias in the ResNet50 feature space, limited sample size for the brain-to-feature model, errors in the conditioning algorithm, and variability due to subjects' mental attention states.
future_direction: Investigate the role of mental attention in modulating neural representations of semantic concepts during visual processing.
Develop models capable of decoding intra-subject activity to enable large-scale decoding on new subjects with minimal fine-tuning.
Decode imagery activity (images seen by the mind's eye), raising ethical considerations but enabling new applications.
Employ other brain imaging modalities (EEG or MEG) to study the temporal dynamics of neural semantic representations.
Use multi-modal data fusion methods combining fMRI with behavioral data or natural language descriptions.
papers.abstract: Brain decoding is a field of computational neuroscience that uses measurable brain activity to infer mental states or internal representations of perceptual inputs. Therefore, we propose a novel approach to brain decoding that also relies on semantic and contextual similarity. We employ an fMRI dataset of natural image vision and create a deep learning decoding pipeline inspired by the existence of both bottom-up and top-down processes in human vision. We train a linear brain-to-feature model to map fMRI activity features to visual stimuli features, assuming that the brain projects visual information onto a space that is homeomorphic to the latent space represented by the last convolutional layer of a pretrained convolutional neural network, which typically collects a variety of semantic features that summarize and highlight similarities and differences between concepts. These features are then categorized in the latent space using a nearest-neighbor strategy, and the results are used to condition a generative latent diffusion model to create novel images. From fMRI data only, we produce reconstructions of visual stimuli that match the original content very well on a semantic level, surpassing the state of the art in previous literature. We evaluate our work and obtain good results using a quantitative semantic metric (the Wu-Palmer similarity metric over the WordNet lexicon, which had an average value of 0.57) and perform a human evaluation experiment that resulted in correct evaluation, according to the multiplicity of human criteria in evaluating image similarity, in over 80% of the test set.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: MoEfication: Transformer Feed-forward Layers are Mixtures of Experts
papers.research_question: Do functional partitions emerge in feed-forward networks (FFNs) of pre-trained Transformers, similar to mixtures of experts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that feed-forward networks in Transformers are naturally mixtures of experts and introduces MoEfication, a method to convert standard models into MoE versions, enabling efficient inference with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The work verifies that Transformer FFNs are mixtures of experts and that MoEfication can convert models to MoE versions for efficient inference and provide insights into FFN mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in pre-trained Transformers exhibit sparse activation, with most inputs activating only a tiny fraction of neurons.
MoEfication can maintain over 95% of original performance while using only 10-30% of FFN parameters.
MoEfication significantly reduces inference FLOPS, achieving up to 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters.
Routing patterns in MoEfied models reveal both general experts (used for most inputs) and input-specific experts (seldom used).
Larger models have sparser activations, making MoEfication more effective for them.
future_direction: Explaining the sparse activation phenomenon empirically or theoretically.
Inspiring future work on the design and training of MoE models.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that feed-forward networks (FFNs) in pre-trained Transformers are a key component, storing various linguistic and factual knowledge. However, the computational patterns of FFNs are still unclear. In this work, we study the computational patterns of FFNs and observe that most inputs only activate a tiny ratio of neurons of FFNs. This phenomenon is similar to the sparsity of the human brain, which drives research on functional partitions of the human brain. To verify whether functional partitions also emerge in FFNs, we propose to convert a model into its MoE version with the same parameters, namely MoEfication. Specifically, MoEfication consists of two phases: (1) splitting the parameters of FFNs into multiple functional partitions as experts, and (2) building expert routers to decide which experts will be used for each input. Experimental results show that MoEfication can conditionally use 10% to 30% of FFN parameters while maintaining over 95% original performance for different models on various downstream tasks. Besides, MoEfication brings two advantages: (1) it significantly reduces the FLOPS of inference, i.e., 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters, and (2) it provides a fine-grained perspective to study the inner mechanism of FFNs. The source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/ thunlp/MoEfication.

papers.title: A Concept-Based Explainability Framework for Large Multimodal Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal representations of large multimodal models (LMMs) by extracting semantically grounded multimodal concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel concept-based explainability framework (CoX-LMM) that uses dictionary learning to extract multimodal concepts from LMM token representations, which are semantically grounded in both vision and text.
papers.conclusion: The CoX-LMM framework successfully extracts multimodal concepts from LMMs, providing a novel way to understand their internal representations and demonstrating the multimodal nature of token representations in these models.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Semi-NMF dictionary learning method extracts multimodal concepts that are semantically meaningful and useful for interpreting test samples.
Semi-NMF achieves a better balance between concept quality (high CLIPScore/BERTScore) and concept disentanglement (low overlap) compared to PCA, K-Means, and a simple baseline.
The extracted concepts demonstrate that token representations in deep layers of the LLM component of an LMM encode multimodal information that can be grounded in both visual and textual domains.
papers.limitation:
The concept dictionaries are token-specific; learning shared concepts across different tokens remains to be explored.
The study is conducted mainly on visual captioning models; generalization to other types of LMMs needs confirmation.
The concept grounding techniques (visual and textual) are simple and could be enhanced.
The evaluation metrics (CLIPScore, BERTScore) have imperfections and are affected by the underlying models.
future_direction: Explore learning concept dictionaries that encode shared concepts for different tokens.
Apply the approach to other types of large multimodal models beyond captioning.
Improve visual and textual grounding techniques, e.g., better localization or using methods like the tuned lens.
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) combine unimodal encoders and large language models (LLMs) to perform multimodal tasks. Despite recent advancements towards the interpretability of these models, understanding internal representations of LMMs remains largely a mystery. In this paper, we present a novel framework for the interpretation of LMMs. We propose a dictionary learning based approach, applied to the representation of tokens. The elements of the learned dictionary correspond to our proposed concepts. We show that these concepts are well semantically grounded in both vision and text. Thus we refer to these as ``multi-modal concepts''. We qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the results of the learnt concepts. We show that the extracted multimodal concepts are useful to interpret representations of test samples.
