papers.conclusion: MFM effectively factorizes multimodal representations into independent discriminative and generative factors, achieving strong performance, generative capabilities, robustness to missing modalities, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on six multimodal datasets.
MFM enables flexible generation of data by conditioning on independent factors and can reconstruct missing modalities without significant performance drop.
Factorizing representations into discriminative and generative factors is crucial for improved performance, as shown in ablation studies.
MFM's representations are interpretable via information-based and gradient-based methods, revealing contributions of different factors.
MFM generalizes well when integrated with other multimodal discriminative models.
future_direction: Extensions of MFM for video generation
Semi-supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
papers.abstract: Learning multimodal representations is a fundamentally complex research problem due to the presence of multiple heterogeneous sources of information. Although the presence of multiple modalities provides additional valuable information, there are two key challenges to address when learning from multimodal data: 1) models must learn the complex intra-modal and cross-modal interactions for prediction and 2) models must be robust to unexpected missing or noisy modalities during testing. In this paper, we propose to optimize for a joint generative-discriminative objective across multimodal data and labels. We introduce a model that factorizes representations into two sets of independent factors: multimodal discriminative and modality-specific generative factors. Multimodal discriminative factors are shared across all modalities and contain joint multimodal features required for discriminative tasks such as sentiment prediction. Modality-specific generative factors are unique for each modality and contain the information required for generating data. Experimental results show that our model is able to learn meaningful multimodal representations that achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance on six multimodal datasets. Our model demonstrates flexible generative capabilities by conditioning on independent factors and can reconstruct missing modalities without significantly impacting performance. Lastly, we interpret our factorized representations to understand the interactions that influence multimodal learning.

papers.title: Do Neural Network Cross-Modal Mappings Really Bridge Modalities?
papers.research_question: Do neural network cross-modal mappings successfully bridge modalities by making the predicted vectors similar to the target vectors in terms of neighborhood structure?
papers.core_contribution: Neural network cross-modal mappings produce mapped vectors whose neighborhood structure resembles the input vectors more than the target vectors, and untrained networks also preserve the input's semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: Neural network cross-modal mappings do not fully bridge modalities as expected, and the semantic structure of the input is preserved in the mapped vectors, advocating for semantic-based evaluation measures.
papers.key_findings:
The neighborhood structure of mapped vectors consistently resembles more that of the input vectors than that of the target vectors.
Untrained networks do not significantly disrupt the neighborhood (semantic) structure of the input vectors.
The proposed mNNO measure provides a more realistic estimate of semantic similarity between predicted and target vectors than geometric measures like MSE.
future_direction: Encouraging the development of better architectures to bridge modalities/spaces.
Advocating for the use of semantic-based criteria to evaluate the quality of predicted vectors.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward networks are widely used in cross-modal applications to bridge modalities by mapping distributed vectors of one modality to the other, or to a shared space. The predicted vectors are then used to perform e.g., retrieval or labeling. Thus, the success of the whole system relies on the ability of the mapping to make the neighborhood structure (i.e., the pairwise similarities) of the predicted vectors akin to that of the target vectors. However, whether this is achieved has not been investigated yet. Here, we propose a new similarity measure and two ad hoc experiments to shed light on this issue. In three cross-modal benchmarks we learn a large number of language-to-vision and visionto-language neural network mappings (up to five layers) using a rich diversity of image and text features and loss functions. Our results reveal that, surprisingly, the neighborhood structure of the predicted vectors consistently resembles more that of the input vectors than that of the target vectors. In a second experiment, we further show that untrained nets do not significantly disrupt the neighborhood (i.e., semantic) structure of the input vectors.

papers.title: Representation Potentials of Foundation Models for Multimodal Alignment: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes evidence for the representation potentials of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within and across modalities, and analyzes the key factors driving this potential.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes substantial evidence for the representation potential of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within individual modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to neuroscience. It analyzes the key factors that foster representation potentials and discusses open questions.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment.
Scale, architectural inductive biases, training objectives, and task and instruction diversity are key factors that foster representation potentials for alignment.
Evidence for alignment is found within vision, language, and speech modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to representations observed in neuroscience.
papers.limitation:
Differences across modalities constrain the extent to which their representations can perfectly align, as certain information may be unique to a given sensory channel.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the effectiveness and interpretability of alignment metrics, and the absence of a universally accepted standard complicates cross-study comparisons.
Training data biases and sociotechnical context shape representation spaces and constrain the universality of alignment claims.
future_direction: Pursue a deeper theoretical grounding of representation potentials.
Develop more robust evaluation frameworks for alignment.
papers.abstract: Foundation models learn highly transferable representations through large-scale pretraining on diverse data. An increasing body of research indicates that these representations exhibit a remarkable degree of similarity across architectures and modalities. In this survey, we investigate the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities. We begin by reviewing representative foundation models and the key metrics that make alignment measurable. We then synthesize empirical evidence of representation potentials from studies in vision, language, speech, multimodality, and neuroscience. The evidence suggests that foundation models often exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment. We further analyze the key factors that foster representation potentials, discuss open questions, and highlight potential challenges.

papers.title: Explaining How Visual, Textual and Multimodal Encoders Share Concepts
papers.research_question: To what extent do visual, textual, and multimodal encoders share internal concepts or features, and can this sharing be quantified and compared across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces wMPPC (weighted Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation) and Comparative Sharedness, two novel indicators for quantitatively comparing concept-level similarities between neural network encoders across different modalities (vision, text, multimodal).
papers.conclusion: The introduced wMPPC and Comparative Sharedness indicators enable a systematic, concept-level comparison of encoders across modalities, revealing that text pretraining significantly impacts the visual features learned by VLMs, which are shared with text encoders.
papers.key_findings:
Shared information between models of different modalities is found mostly in the last layer of each model.
wMPPC reveals differences in image-text alignment quality between datasets (e.g., COCO vs. Laion-2B).
A typology of visual concepts specific to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is identified, including age-related features, pets with unusual behavior, rooms, vehicles, old photos, geographical features, and features related to the verb 'to ride'.
Visual features specific to VLMs are also better shared with text encoders than with visual foundation models, highlighting the impact of text pretraining on image understanding.
The proposed tools enable systematic, large-scale comparative analysis of 21 encoders across three modalities.
papers.limitation:
All models studied are transformer-based; convolutional or hierarchical models with large feature maps are not considered.
Only encoder models are considered, not decoders or generative models.
wMPPC is asymmetric and does not constitute a proper distance metric.
Sparse autoencoders are not guaranteed to extract every single concept used by a model.
future_direction: Using wMPPC to assess the image-text alignment quality of datasets for training model selection or filtering.
Developing techniques for automatically naming SAE features using both images and captions to enable large-scale Comparative Sharedness analysis.
Extending the systematic wMPPC analysis to generative models of different modalities.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for extracting human-interpretable features from neural networks activations. Previous works compared different models based on SAE-derived features but those comparisons have been restricted to models within the same modality. We propose a novel indicator allowing quantitative comparison of models across SAE features, and use it to conduct a comparative study of visual, textual and multimodal encoders. We also propose to quantify the Comparative Sharedness of individual features between different classes of models. With these two new tools, we conduct several studies on 21 encoders of the three types, with two significantly different sizes, and considering generalist and domain specific datasets. The results allow to revisit previous studies at the light of encoders trained in a multimodal context and to quantify to which extent all these models share some representations or features. They also suggest that visual features that are specific to VLMs among vision encoders are shared with text encoders, highlighting the impact of text pretraining. The code is available at https://github.com/CEA-LIST/SAEshareConcepts

papers.title: The Representational Alignment Hypothesis: Evidence for and Consequences of Invariant Semantic Structure Across Embedding Modalities
papers.research_question: Is there an underlying invariant semantic structure common to independently trained representation spaces (e.g., neural, textual, visual, auditory)? If so, is it an inherent property of meaning, or does it reflect shared biological, environmental, and cultural conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper surveys evidence for the Representational Alignment Hypothesis (RAH), which posits an invariant semantic structure across embedding modalities, and argues against the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, offering alternative explanations rooted in metasemantics.
papers.conclusion: The paper reviews evidence for the Representational Alignment Hypothesis and argues against the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, suggesting the invariant structure may reflect human-specific conditions rather than fundamental reality.
papers.key_findings:
Two complementary research strands (transformation-based approaches and internal structure comparison methods) provide converging evidence that independently trained embeddings from text, vision, audio, and neural signals can exhibit a shared semantic organization.
Simple linear transformations can align embeddings with minimal supervision, suggesting the underlying geometries are 'near-isomorphic.'
Purely geometric or relational analyses (e.g., RSA, topological data analysis) reveal strong cross-modal parallels in how items cluster or correlate.
The observed alignment might stem from shared data-generating conditions (human biology, culture, environment) rather than a fundamental, Platonic reality.
papers.limitation:
The invariant structure might arise from the embedding algorithms themselves, not from an inherent property of meaning.
The alignment might reflect how the human brain processes information, imposing its own constraints and biases on any data.
The semantic structure identified might be specific to Earth's unique biological and environmental context, not universally invariant.
future_direction: Constructing simulated environments where underlying 'semantic' factors are controlled to test the emergence of invariant representations.
Cross-cultural and cross-species comparisons to test the depth and universality of the alignments.
Developing new interpretability methods to reveal which semantic attributes drive alignment across modalities.
papers.abstract: There is growing evidence that independently trained AI systems come to represent the world in the same way. In other words, independently trained embeddings from text, vision, audio, and neural signals share an underlying geometry. We call this the Representational Alignment Hypothesis (RAH) and investigate evidence for and consequences of this claim. The evidence is of two kinds: (i) internal structure comparison techniques, such as representational similarity analysis and topological data analysis, reveal matching relational patterns across modalities without explicit mapping; and (ii) methods based on cross-modal embedding alignment, which learn mappings between representation spaces, show that simple linear transformations can bring different embedding spaces into close correspondence, suggesting near-isomorphism. Taken together, the evidence suggests that, even after controlling for trivial commonalities inherent in standard data preprocessing and embedding procedures, a robust structural correspondence persists, hinting at an underlying organizational principle. Some have argued that this result shows that the shared structure is getting at a fundamental, Platonic level of reality. We argue that this conclusion is unjustified. Moreover, we aim to give the idea an alternative philosophical home, rooted in contemporary metasemantics (i.e., theories of what makes a representation and what makes something meaningful) and responses to the symbol grounding problem. We conclude by considering the scope of the RAH and proposing new ways of distinguishing semantic structures that are genuinely invariant from those that inevitably arise due to the fact that all our data is generated under human-specific conditions on Earth.

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
Affine mappings can be learned between the hidden states of small and large models from the same family.
Steering vectors learned on small models retain their semantic effect when transferred to large models via the learned affine map.
The transferred steering vectors are as effective as those learned directly on the large model for tasks like refusal behavior removal and logit-based evaluation.
The feature spaces of models, as represented by sparse autoencoder decoder matrices, are approximately linearly related.
The conceptual framework of a universal representation space provides a plausible explanation for the linear transferability.
papers.limitation:
The limits of transferability across very different model sizes (e.g., 100M to 70B) are not yet understood.
Transferability across different model families or architectures is challenging due to differences in tokenization schemes and architectural design.
future_direction: Investigating the limits of transferability across model sizes.
Exploring transferability across different model families and architectures.
Developing theoretical foundations for the LRT hypothesis and the universal representation space.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that neural networks with similar architectures trained on similar data learn shared representations relevant to the learning task. We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: Quantifying Modality Contributions via Disentangling Multimodal Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the contributions of individual modalities in multimodal models, separating inherent informativeness from cross-modal interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a PID-based framework and an efficient IPFP algorithm to quantify modality contributions in multimodal models by decomposing predictive information into unique, redundant, and synergistic components.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a principled PID-based framework for quantifying modality contributions in multimodal models, providing a scalable, model-agnostic, and performance-independent tool for analyzing multimodal interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed PID-based metric accurately captures modality contributions on synthetic data, matching theoretical expectations for binary bitwise operations.
On balanced multimodal tasks (VQA, GQA), models show relatively balanced modality contributions (approximately 55% text, 45% image).
On ScienceQA, text contributions are slightly higher, and on NLVR2, image contributions increase for most models, reflecting task-specific modality reliance.
Ablation studies show that fusion method significantly affects modality contributions; bidirectional fusion and concatenation yield more balanced contributions than unidirectional cross-attention.
Input perturbations (e.g., noisy images, jumbled text) consistently shift modality contributions, indicating the model's sensitivity to disruptions in each modality.
papers.limitation:
The PID estimates are sensitive to noise in the embedding space.
The method may not be fully immune to spurious correlations in the data or model representations.
The approach assumes access to intermediate model embeddings, which may not be available for closed-source or API-restricted systems.
future_direction: Improving robustness to noise in the embedding space.
Mitigating the influence of spurious correlations in the data or model representations.
papers.abstract: Quantifying modality contributions in multimodal models remains a challenge, as existing approaches conflate the notion of contribution itself. Prior work relies on accuracy-based approaches, interpreting performance drops after removing a modality as indicative of its influence. However, such outcome-driven metrics fail to distinguish whether a modality is inherently informative or whether its value arises only through interaction with other modalities. This distinction is particularly important in cross-attention architectures, where modalities influence each other's representations. In this work, we propose a framework based on Partial Information Decomposition (PID) that quantifies modality contributions by decomposing predictive information in internal embeddings into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. To enable scalable, inference-only analysis, we develop an algorithm based on the Iterative Proportional Fitting Procedure (IPFP) that computes layer and dataset-level contributions without retraining. This provides a principled, representation-level view of multimodal behavior, offering clearer and more interpretable insights than outcome-based metrics.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Transformer-Exclusive Cross-Modal Representation for Vision and Language
papers.research_question: Can cross-modal representation for vision and language be tackled exclusively with transformer architecture, without using CNNs or RNNs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a transformer-exclusive cross-modal model for vision and language tasks, demonstrating comparable performance to state-of-the-art models without additional cross-modal pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The transformer-exclusive approach for cross-modal tasks shows potential, and performance can be improved with larger models, more sophisticated embedding schemes, and additional pre-training data.
papers.key_findings:
The transformer-exclusive model achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art cross-modal models without additional cross-modal pre-training.
The model outperforms combinations of CNN+BERT and ViT+LSTM under the same conditions (no cross-modal pre-training and simple concatenation).
Architectural integrity (using the same transformer architecture for both modalities) may play an important role in learning cross-modal representations.
The model is smaller in parameters compared to other models because it eliminates the need for an external region detector.
papers.limitation:
The model does not achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to models that use additional cross-modal pre-training.
The model uses a simple concatenation scheme and small baseline models, which may limit performance.
A more thorough study is required to conclusively claim that ViT is superior to ResNet or that attention is superior to convolution.
future_direction: Using larger pre-trained models to enhance performance.
Using more sophisticated common embedding schemes to improve performance.
Using additional cross-modal pre-training data to boost performance.
papers.abstract: Ever since the advent of deep learning, crossmodal representation learning has been dominated by the approaches involving convolutional neural networks for visual representation and recurrent neural networks for language representation. Transformer architecture, however, has rapidly taken over the recurrent neural networks in natural language processing tasks, and it has also been shown that vision tasks can be handled with transformer architecture, with compatible performance to convolutional neural networks. Such results naturally lead to speculation upon the possibility of tackling cross-modal representation for vision and language exclusively with transformer. This paper examines transformerexclusive cross-modal representation to explore such possibility, demonstrating its potentials as well as discussing its current limitations and its prospects.

papers.title: Vision-Language Integration in Multimodal Video Transformers (Partially) Aligns with the Brain
papers.research_question: To what extent do multimodal video transformers learn brain-relevant cross-modal connections and interactions between vision and language?
papers.core_contribution: This work probes a multimodal video transformer using brain recordings, finding that cross-modal representations can improve alignment with language brain regions, but pre-trained models lack brain-relevant multimodal interactions, which can be improved by fine-tuning on a vision-language inference task.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal video transformers partially align with brain-relevant vision-language integration, with cross-modal connections benefiting individual modalities, but capturing full multimodal interactions may require task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Vision-language representations significantly improve brain alignment with language regions over language-only representations, particularly in the angular gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, and posterior cingulate cortex.
The improved alignment in the angular gyrus is largely attributable to the model's use of visual information for masked language prediction.
No evidence was found that the pre-trained model captures brain-relevant multimodal interactions beyond the sum of individual modalities.
Fine-tuning the model on a vision-language question-answering task (TVQA) improved brain alignment in the angular gyrus and led to evidence of brain-relevant multimodal interactions.
The top layers of the fine-tuned model showed decreased brain alignment but increased task accuracy, suggesting these layers encode task-specific information not present in passive viewing brain data.
papers.limitation:
The study investigates only one type of multimodal video model (MERLOT Reserve) and uses one brain dataset (Courtois Friends TV show fMRI dataset).
The TVQA dataset may have unimodal biases, where some questions can be answered using only one modality.
future_direction: Study the brain relevance of a larger variety of multimodal video models as more become publicly available.
Scale up the approach to multiple multimodal brain datasets.
Leverage the brain to identify examples that require vision-language integration to create a more challenging multi-modal benchmark dataset.
papers.abstract: Integrating information from multiple modalities is arguably one of the essential prerequisites for grounding artificial intelligence systems with an understanding of the real world. Recent advances in video transformers that jointly learn from vision, text, and sound over time have made some progress toward this goal, but the degree to which these models integrate information from modalities still remains unclear. In this work, we present a promising approach for probing a pre-trained multimodal video transformer model by leveraging neuroscientific evidence of multimodal information processing in the brain. Using brain recordings of participants watching a popular TV show, we analyze the effects of multi-modal connections and interactions in a pre-trained multi-modal video transformer on the alignment with uni- and multi-modal brain regions. We find evidence that vision enhances masked prediction performance during language processing, providing support that cross-modal representations in models can benefit individual modalities. However, we don't find evidence of brain-relevant information captured by the joint multi-modal transformer representations beyond that captured by all of the individual modalities. We finally show that the brain alignment of the pre-trained joint representation can be improved by fine-tuning using a task that requires vision-language inferences. Overall, our results paint an optimistic picture of the ability of multi-modal transformers to integrate vision and language in partially brain-relevant ways but also show that improving the brain alignment of these models may require new approaches.

papers.title: From Words to Waves: Analyzing Concept Formation in Speech and Text-Based Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do conceptual structures in speech models differ from those in text and multimodal models, and to what extent do different modalities yield shared or modality-specific semantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares conceptual structures in speech, text, and multimodal models, finding that text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models exhibit unique alignment due to cross-modal training.
papers.conclusion: Text models directly encode linguistic structures from early layers, speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models show unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
papers.key_findings:
Text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually transition from acoustic to linguistic representations.
Multimodal models like SpeechT5 exhibit unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
Speech models allocate less capacity to linguistic and semantic taxonomies, focusing more on speech-specific features like phonetics.
Speech models show weaker performance in capturing negative sentiment compared to text models in task-specific tests.
papers.limitation:
Speech models struggle with tasks requiring deep linguistic reasoning compared to text-based models.
Speech-based sentiment classifiers have difficulty capturing negative sentiment effectively.
future_direction: Integrating additional linguistic or prosodic cues in speech-based models.
Leveraging multi-modal learning strategies.
Exploring alternative architectures to better capture nuances of spoken sentiment.
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated that systems trained solely on text can acquire extensive world knowledge, develop reasoning capabilities, and internalize abstract semantic concepts--showcasing properties that can be associated with general intelligence. This raises an intriguing question: Do such concepts emerge in models trained on other modalities, such as speech? Furthermore, when models are trained jointly on multiple modalities: Do they develop a richer, more structured semantic understanding? To explore this, we analyze the conceptual structures learned by speech and textual models both individually and jointly. We employ Latent Concept Analysis, an unsupervised method for uncovering and interpreting latent representations in neural networks, to examine how semantic abstractions form across modalities. For reproducibility we made scripts and other resources available to the community.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: Seeing What Tastes Good: Revisiting Multimodal Distributional Semantics in the Billion Parameter Era
papers.research_question: How well do large-scale vision, language, and multimodal models represent semantic attributes of concrete object concepts? Which attributes are salient for each modality?
papers.core_contribution: Multimodal vision encoders outperform single-modality models on predicting semantic attributes, but vision-only and language-only models also show strong performance, indicating convergence across modalities.
papers.conclusion: Multimodally-trained vision encoders represent conceptual attributes better than single-modality encoders, but single-modality encoders still perform well, and overall correlations are high, indicating convergence across modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Multimodal vision encoders (e.g., SigLIP, PaliGemma) are amongst the highest performing models across both semantic attribute datasets.
Text-only large language models (Gemma, DeBERTa v3) also rank highly, especially on the Binder attribute ratings.
Self-supervised vision models (Swin-V2, DINOv2) learn substantial conceptual attribute knowledge, comparable to modern LLMs, despite no access to lexical information.
Label-supervised vision models (Max ViT) perform worse than self-supervised models, suggesting label supervision may be harmful for learning human-aligned attributes.
All performant models show high correlations across modalities, indicating a degree of convergence in conceptual representation.
papers.limitation: Linear probes might learn correlated attributes rather than the target attribute, e.g., due to attribute extensions coinciding with taxonomic supercategories.
future_direction: Investigating the predictive power and utility of probing tasks for multimodal training.
Extending beyond simple object concepts to more abstract, situational, and configurational concepts.
papers.abstract: Human learning and conceptual representation is grounded in sensorimotor experience, in contrast to state-of-the-art foundation models. In this paper, we investigate how well such large-scale models, trained on vast quantities of data, represent the semantic feature norms of concrete object concepts, e.g. a ROSE is red, smells sweet, and is a flower. More specifically, we use probing tasks to test which properties of objects these models are aware of. We evaluate image encoders trained on image data alone, as well as multimodally-trained image encoders and language-only models, on predicting an extended denser version of the classic McRae norms and the newer Binder dataset of attribute ratings. We find that multimodal image encoders slightly outperform language-only approaches, and that image-only encoders perform comparably to the language models, even on non-visual attributes that are classified as "encyclopedic" or "function". These results offer new insights into what can be learned from pure unimodal learning, and the complementarity of the modalities.

papers.title: Multimodal Neurons in Pretrained Text-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: Can the crossmodal generalization ability of language models be traced to individual neurons? Does translation between modalities occur in the projection layer or deeper within the transformer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in a vision-language model with a frozen text transformer, multimodal neurons emerge in the transformer MLPs that convert visual representations into corresponding text, and that translation between modalities occurs inside the transformer, not in the projection layer.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal neurons exist in text-only transformer MLPs and consistently translate image semantics into language. Translation between modalities happens inside the transformer, not in the projection layer.
papers.key_findings:
Image prompts cast into the transformer embedding space do not encode interpretable semantics; translation between modalities occurs inside the transformer.
Multimodal neurons can be found within the transformer MLPs, and they are active in response to particular image semantics.
Multimodal neurons causally affect output: ablating them can remove concepts from image captions.
Multimodal neurons are selective for specific visual concepts across inputs, as measured by IoU with object segmentations.
The decoded text from multimodal neurons agrees with image semantics, as measured by CLIPScore and BERTScore.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single multimodal model (LiMBeR-BEIT) with separately learned vision and language components.
The knowledge of the structure of vector spaces representing information from different modalities remains incomplete, and how concepts encoded by individual units are assembled from upstream representations is not investigated.
future_direction: Investigate the phenomenon of multimodal neurons in other vision-language architectures and models aligning other modalities.
Explore whether similar neurons emerge when the visual encoder is replaced with a raw pixel stream or a pretrained speech autoencoder.
Build a more mechanistic understanding of information processing within transformers to explain their ability to generalize to non-textual representations.
papers.abstract: Language models demonstrate remarkable capacity to generalize representations learned in one modality to downstream tasks in other modalities. Can we trace this ability to individual neurons? We study the case where a frozen text transformer is augmented with vision using a self-supervised visual encoder and a single linear projection learned on an image-to-text task. Outputs of the projection layer are not immediately decodable into language describing image content; instead, we find that translation between modalities occurs deeper within the transformer. We introduce a procedure for identifying "multimodal neurons" that convert visual representations into corresponding text, and decoding the concepts they inject into the model's residual stream. In a series of experiments, we show that multimodal neurons operate on specific visual concepts across inputs, and have a systematic causal effect on image captioning.

papers.title: Abstraction Induces the Brain Alignment of Language and Speech Models
papers.research_question: Why do intermediate hidden states of language and speech models predict brain responses? Is this due to shared meaning abstraction rather than next-word prediction properties?
papers.core_contribution: The correspondence between speech/language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction, not next-word prediction. The intrinsic dimension of representations peaks in intermediate layers and strongly predicts brain encoding performance.
papers.conclusion: Meaning abstraction, as captured by high intrinsic dimension, is the key driver of model-brain similarity, and prediction objectives alone are insufficient for achieving this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Layerwise surprisal does not account for layerwise encoding performance, ruling out next-token predictivity as the primary driver.
Intrinsic dimension (Id) peaks in intermediate layers and tracks the construction of higher-order linguistic features (semantic abstraction).
Layerwise Id strongly correlates with layerwise brain encoding performance across models and imaging modalities.
Id and encoding performance grow in tandem over model pre-training, indicating the relationship emerges from learning.
Finetuning models to better predict brain activity causally increases both the Id and semantic content of their representations.
papers.limitation:
High intrinsic dimension is necessary but not sufficient for high neural predictivity, as demonstrated by random Fourier features.
The relationship between Id and encoding performance is weaker for some speech models (e.g., WavLM-base-plus) where low-level acoustic similarity may dominate.
future_direction: Developing better methods for extracting task-relevant structure from naturalistic data to advance encoding models.
Further investigation of linear dimensionality measures in relation to abstraction and encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models and speech audio models predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most effective for this unique and highly general transfer task? We give evidence that the correspondence between speech and language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction and not their next-word prediction properties. In particular, models construct higher-order linguistic features in their middle layers, cued by a peak in the layerwise intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity. We show that a layer's intrinsic dimension strongly predicts how well it explains fMRI and ECoG signals; that the relation between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity arises over model pre-training; and finetuning models to better predict the brain causally increases both representations' intrinsic dimension and their semantic content. Results suggest that semantic richness, high intrinsic dimension, and brain predictivity mirror each other, and that the key driver of model-brain similarity is rich meaning abstraction of the inputs, where language modeling is a task sufficiently complex (but perhaps not the only) to require it.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers
papers.research_question: What enables transformers to perform multimodal ICL, both in terms of training data statistics and mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a learning asymmetry in multimodal ICL where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers a learning asymmetry where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE increases the data complexity threshold for ICL emergence.
Multimodal ICL exhibits a learning asymmetry: with high-diversity primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices.
Scaling up unimodal models favors in-weight memorization over ICL, but scaling improves multimodal ICL.
Multimodal ICL relies on induction-style mechanisms that copy labels from matching in-context exemplars.
Encoders improve multimodal ICL by aligning features and providing discriminative representations.
papers.limitation: Observations on production MLLMs are not intended as a mechanistic explanation due to vastly more complex training regimes, data distributions, and architectural choices that confound clean attribution.
future_direction: Investigate circuit-level robustness.
Explore architectural designs that inherently favor robust reasoning over memorization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this question through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) increases the data complexity threshold for ICL. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
Cholinergic modulation is a common mechanism that biases processing toward external modes across multiple systems.
future_direction: Test the prediction that disruption of mode-switching (e.g., between non-REM and REM sleep) impairs integration of new hippocampal memories with existing neocortical knowledge.
Investigate how altering the timescale of switching affects the learning of temporally extended features.
Explore the role of neuromodulators like acetylcholine in regulating mode-switching and learning across different brain systems.
papers.abstract: Brains construct internal models that support perception, prediction, and action in the external world. Individual circuits within a brain also learn internal models of the local world of input they receive, in order to facilitate efficient and robust representation. How are these internal models learned? We propose that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing. We review computational evidence that this mode-switching can produce an error signal to drive learning. We then consider empirical evidence for the instantiation of mode-switching in diverse neural systems, ranging from subsecond fluctuations in the hippocampus to wake-sleep alternations across the whole brain. We hypothesize that these internal/external switching processes, which occur at multiple scales, can drive learning at each scale. This framework predicts that (a) slower mode-switching should be associated with learning of more temporally extended input features and (b) disruption of switching should impair the integration of new information with prior information.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: Cross-modal Associations in Vision and Language Models: Revisiting the Bouba-Kiki Effect
papers.research_question: Do vision-and-language models (VLMs) exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, specifically the bouba-kiki effect?
papers.core_contribution: CLIP models (ResNet and ViT) do not show consistent human-like cross-modal associations (bouba-kiki effect), and their internal representations lack the robust modality integration seen in humans.
papers.conclusion: VLMs do not exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.
papers.key_findings:
Neither CLIP ResNet nor ViT consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect across different prompts and pseudoword sets.
Models can correctly associate English adjectives with corresponding shapes (baseline), but fail for pseudowords.
Grad-CAM analysis shows that models do not attend to shape-specific features when processing pseudowords.
Models' predictions are inconsistent and often collapse to a few labels, indicating lack of robust cross-modal associations.
The models' performance is at chance level for the bouba-kiki task, in contrast to humans who show strong preferences.
papers.limitation:
Only tested on CLIP versions, not on more capable proprietary models.
Relies on text (orthographic) presentation of pseudowords, which may not capture auditory aspects of the bouba-kiki effect.
future_direction: Exploring cross-modal associations in more contemporary models (e.g., those with alignment layers).
Investigating audio-visual models to understand how different modalities contribute.
Incorporating cross-linguistic studies to account for cultural variation.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have raised questions about whether vision-and-language models (VLMs) integrate cross-modal information in ways that reflect human cognition. One well-studied test case in this domain is the bouba-kiki effect, where humans reliably associate pseudowords like `bouba' with round shapes and `kiki' with jagged ones. Given the mixed evidence found in prior studies for this effect in VLMs, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation focused on two variants of CLIP, ResNet and Vision Transformer (ViT), given their centrality in many state-of-the-art VLMs. We apply two complementary methods closely modelled after human experiments: a prompt-based evaluation that uses probabilities as a measure of model preference, and we use Grad-CAM as a novel approach to interpret visual attention in shape-word matching tasks. Our findings show that these model variants do not consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect. While ResNet shows a preference for round shapes, overall performance across both model variants lacks the expected associations. Moreover, direct comparison with prior human data on the same task shows that the models' responses fall markedly short of the robust, modality-integrated behaviour characteristic of human cognition. These results contribute to the ongoing debate about the extent to which VLMs truly understand cross-modal concepts, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Brain2GAN: Feature-disentangled neural encoding and decoding of visual perception in the primate brain
papers.research_question: How do feature-disentangled latent representations of generative models align with neural representations in the primate visual cortex, and can they be used for accurate neural decoding (reconstruction of visual stimuli from brain activity)?
papers.core_contribution: Feature-disentangled w-latents of GANs (StyleGAN) align better with high-level neural representations in the primate visual cortex than other latent representations (z-latents, CLIP-latents) and enable state-of-the-art reconstruction of visual stimuli from brain activity.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the importance of feature disentanglement in explaining high-level neural representations and shows that unsupervised generative models like StyleGAN can serve as effective models for neural coding, with implications for neuroprosthetics and brain-computer interfaces.
papers.key_findings:
w-latents of StyleGAN outperform z-latents and CLIP-latents in predicting neural responses in high-level visual areas (IT cortex).
Neural decoding using w-latents results in high-fidelity reconstructions of both face and natural images from multi-unit activity.
The alignment between w-latents and neural representations suggests a shared encoding principle for visual phenomena, despite the GAN never being trained on neural data.
Time-based decoding reveals the temporal dynamics of information processing across visual areas V1, V4, and IT.
Linear operations applied to decoded w-latents (e.g., interpolation, arithmetic) yield semantically meaningful transformations in the reconstructed images.
papers.limitation: The study used a passive fixation task, which may not reflect natural vision where eye movements and attention play a role.
future_direction: Applying the method to more complex tasks and naturalistic settings.
Integrating the approach with other generative models and neural recording modalities.
Exploring the use of the method for clinical applications such as visual neuroprosthetics.
papers.abstract: A challenging goal of neural coding is to characterize the neural representations underlying visual perception. To this end, multi-unit activity (MUA) of macaque visual cortex was recorded in a passive fixation task upon presentation of faces and natural images. We analyzed the relationship between MUA and latent representations of state-of-the-art deep generative models, including the conventional and feature-disentangled representations of generative adversarial networks (GANs) (i.e., z- and w-latents of StyleGAN, respectively) and language-contrastive representations of latent diffusion networks (i.e., CLIP-latents of Stable Diffusion). A mass univariate neural encoding analysis of the latent representations showed that feature-disentangled w representations outperform both z and CLIP representations in explaining neural responses. Further, w-latent features were found to be positioned at the higher end of the complexity gradient which indicates that they capture visual information relevant to high-level neural activity. Subsequently, a multivariate neural decoding analysis of the feature-disentangled representations resulted in state-of-the-art spatiotemporal reconstructions of visual perception. Taken together, our results not only highlight the important role of feature-disentanglement in shaping high-level neural representations underlying visual perception but also serve as an important benchmark for the future of neural coding.

papers.title: Unambiguous Representations in Neural Networks: An Information-Theoretic Approach to Intentionality
papers.research_question: Can neural networks encode information unambiguously through relational structure, such that a neuron's representational content can be determined from its connectivity patterns alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes representational ambiguity using information theory and demonstrates that relational structures in neural network connectivity can unambiguously encode representational content, with dropout training leading to near-perfect decoding of neuron class identity.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can achieve the unambiguous representations required by theoretical accounts of consciousness through relational structure, and training paradigm significantly affects ambiguity independently of task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout-trained networks achieve perfect (100%) accuracy in decoding output neuron class identity from connectivity patterns using geometric matching, while standard backpropagation networks achieve only 38% accuracy, despite identical task performance.
Spatial position of input neurons can be decoded from connectivity with R2 up to 0.844 for standard backpropagation networks, showing that relational structure encodes low-level positional information.
Representational ambiguity is orthogonal to task performance, as networks with similar classification accuracy exhibit dramatically different levels of ambiguity.
Dataset identity (MNIST vs. Fashion-MNIST) can be classified from relational structure with near-perfect accuracy (99.8%) for dropout networks.
The full relational geometry (global structure) is necessary for accurate decoding; local neighborhood information alone is insufficient.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on simple feedforward networks trained with supervised learning on MNIST, leaving open whether similar unambiguous encoding emerges in more complex scenarios (e.g., unsupervised learning, naturalistic datasets, recurrent networks, deeper architectures).
Measures H(I|R, C) (conditional entropy given context) rather than H(I|R), though evidence suggests context (dataset, architecture) can be inferred from structure.
Analyzes structural connectivity (synaptic weights) rather than functional connectivity (activity correlations), which may be more relevant for consciousness.
Examines single layers in isolation, not how relational structures compose across layers or whether hierarchy introduces or reduces ambiguity.
future_direction: Applying the framework to more complex scenarios: unsupervised or self-supervised learning, naturalistic datasets, recurrent networks with temporal dynamics, or deeper hierarchical architectures.
Analyzing functional connectivity patterns during actual stimulus processing, particularly in biological neural recordings.
Applying the framework to biological neural data to test if low representational ambiguity correlates with conscious perception.
papers.abstract: Representations pervade our daily experience, from letters representing sounds to bit strings encoding digital files. While such representations require externally defined decoders to convey meaning, conscious experience appears fundamentally different: a neural state corresponding to perceiving a red square cannot alternatively encode the experience of a green square.
