This intrinsic property of consciousness suggests that conscious representations must be unambiguous in a way that conventional representations are not. We formalize this intuition using information theory, defining representational ambiguity as the conditional entropy H(I|R) over possible interpretations I given a representation R. Through experiments on neural networks trained to classify MNIST digits, we demonstrate that relational structures in network connectivity can unambiguously encode representational content. Using both learned decoders and direct geometric matching, we achieve perfect (100%) accuracy for dropout-trained networks and 38% for standard backpropagation in identifying output neuron class identity, despite identical task performance, demonstrating that representational ambiguity can arise orthogonally to behavioral accuracy. We further show that spatial position information of input neurons can be decoded from network connectivity with R2 up to 0.844. These results provide a quantitative method for measuring representational ambiguity in neural systems and demonstrate that neural networks can exhibit the low-ambiguity representations posited as necessary (though not sufficient) by theoretical accounts of consciousness.

papers.title: Attention as Grounding: Exploring Textual and Cross-Modal Attention on Entities and Relations in Language-and-Vision Transformer
papers.research_question: Does attention across two modalities learn visually grounded semantics of nouns? What syntactic knowledge is encoded in attention on text in the multi-modal set-up? What does cross-modal attention learn about grounded semantics of spatial relations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in a multi-modal transformer, cross-modal attention learns visual grounding of noun phrases and semantic information about spatial relations, while masked self-attention captures syntactic dependencies between words.
papers.conclusion: The language model in a multi-modal task captures linguistic phenomena of different kinds depending on the source knowledge (text or objects) and semantic type of the output words (noun phrases or spatial relations).
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal attention in deeper layers specializes in visually grounding noun phrases to objects.
Masked self-attention captures syntactic dependencies between words, with a clear separation between attention on object-related words (determiners, adjectives, nouns) and relation-related words (verbs, adpositions).
Attention patterns for spatial relations show that landmarks are more attended from relations than from targets, and deeper layers in cross-modal attention are more activated for grounding relations.
There is a difference in how objects and relations are grounded cross-modally, with relations being more challenging to ground.
papers.limitation: The way relations are grounded in a transformer model is not completely transparent and is more challenging than grounding nouns.
future_direction: Examining the effect of different feature representations for spatial relations (e.g., RGB-D, geometry models, common sense knowledge) and models built around them.
Examining grounding of relations in a different task, such as vision-and-language navigation.
papers.abstract: We explore how a multi-modal transformer trained for generation of longer image descriptions learns syntactic and semantic representations about entities and relations grounded in objects at the level of masked self-attention (text generation) and crossmodal attention (information fusion). We observe that cross-attention learns the visual grounding of noun phrases into objects and high-level semantic information about spatial relations, while text-to-text attention captures low-level syntactic knowledge between words. This concludes that language models in a multi-modal task learn different semantic information about objects and relations cross-modally and uni-modally (text-only).

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods for Multisensory Integration in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How do early training dynamics affect a neural network's ability to integrate information from multiple sources, and do deep networks exhibit critical learning periods for multisensory integration similar to biological systems?
papers.core_contribution: Deep networks exhibit critical learning periods for multisensory integration where early exposure to properly correlated signals is crucial, and cross-sensor reconstruction objectives can make learning more robust to such periods.
papers.conclusion: Critical learning periods for multi-source integration exist in deep networks across architectures and tasks, and training should be performed across modalities from the outset rather than pre-training separate backbones.
papers.key_findings:
Deep networks show critical learning periods for multisensory integration: temporary deficits early in training can permanently impair the ability to integrate sources.
Shallow networks do not exhibit such critical periods.
Even deep linear networks exhibit critical periods, indicating complex early dynamics contrary to wide-network linearization theories.
The introduced Relative Source Variance (RSV) measure reveals that deficits lead to polarized representations where units become selective to only one source.
Auxiliary cross-sensor reconstruction objectives stabilize learning dynamics and prevent critical periods, suggesting a reason for the success of self-supervised multi-modal training.
papers.limitation: The study focused on homogeneous sources (stereo, video) and did not investigate asymmetry between sources (e.g., different informativeness or ease).
future_direction: Study the role of asymmetry between sources (e.g., different informativeness or ease).
papers.abstract: We show that the ability of a neural network to integrate information from diverse sources hinges critically on being exposed to properly correlated signals during the early phases of training. Interfering with the learning process during this initial stage can permanently impair the development of a skill, both in artificial and biological systems where the phenomenon is known as a critical learning period. We show that critical periods arise from the complex and unstable early transient dynamics, which are decisive of final performance of the trained system and their learned representations. This evidence challenges the view, engendered by analysis of wide and shallow networks, that early learning dynamics of neural networks are simple, akin to those of a linear model. Indeed, we show that even deep linear networks exhibit critical learning periods for multi-source integration, while shallow networks do not. To better understand how the internal representations change according to disturbances or sensory deficits, we introduce a new measure of source sensitivity, which allows us to track the inhibition and integration of sources during training. Our analysis of inhibition suggests cross-source reconstruction as a natural auxiliary training objective, and indeed we show that architectures trained with cross-sensor reconstruction objectives are remarkably more resilient to critical periods. Our findings suggest that the recent success in self-supervised multi-modal training compared to previous supervised efforts may be in part due to more robust learning dynamics and not solely due to better architectures and/or more data.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: One Model, Multiple Modalities: A Sparsely Activated Approach for Text, Sound, Image, Video and Code
papers.research_question: Can a single model with sparsely activated modality-specific parameters handle multiple modalities and perform comparably to modality-specific models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SkillNet, a sparsely activated multimodal model that handles text, sound, image, video, and code with a single model, achieving performance comparable to modality-specific models and better accuracy with fewer activated parameters in some tasks.
papers.conclusion: This paper presents a sparsely activated multimodal multitask approach called SkillNet, demonstrating the feasibility of using one model to achieve comparable performance to multiple modality-specific models, and shows that sparse pretraining leads to improved accuracy, even better than modality-specific pretraining on three of five modalities.
papers.key_findings:
SkillNet without pretraining performs comparably to five modality-specific models.
Pretraining significantly improves SkillNet's performance on all five modalities, on par with or better than baselines with modality-specific pretraining.
On Chinese text-to-image retrieval, SkillNet achieves higher accuracy than existing systems (WukongViT-B and Wenlan 2.0) while using fewer activated parameters.
The dense multimodal baseline performs poorly on low-resource tasks like text-to-video retrieval, but SkillNet and MoE baseline do not have this issue.
SkillNet's sparse activation allows for efficient inference by activating only relevant parameters.
papers.limitation: The model is only evaluated on five modalities and a specific model scale (12 layers, 768 hidden dimensions); extension to more modalities and larger scales is left for future work.
future_direction: Extend to larger number of modalities and tasks
Scale the model to larger sizes (more layers and hidden dimensions)
papers.abstract: People perceive the world with multiple senses (e.g., through hearing sounds, reading words and seeing objects). However, most existing AI systems only process an individual modality. This paper presents an approach that excels at handling multiple modalities of information with a single model. In our "{SkillNet}" model, different parts of the parameters are specialized for processing different modalities. Unlike traditional dense models that always activate all the model parameters, our model sparsely activates parts of the parameters whose skills are relevant to the task. Such model design enables SkillNet to learn skills in a more interpretable way. We develop our model for five modalities including text, image, sound, video and code. Results show that, SkillNet performs comparably to five modality-specific fine-tuned models. Moreover, our model supports self-supervised pretraining with the same sparsely activated way, resulting in better initialized parameters for different modalities. We find that pretraining significantly improves the performance of SkillNet on five modalities, on par with or even better than baselines with modality-specific pretraining. On the task of Chinese text-to-image retrieval, our final system achieves higher accuracy than existing leading systems including Wukong{ViT-B} and Wenlan 2.0 while using less number of activated parameters.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do disentangled representations emerge in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task learning in evidence accumulation tasks leads to disentangled representations in the latent state of autoregressive models, with theoretical guarantees on emergence conditions.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task learning establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, explaining their generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical guarantees show that any optimal multi-task classifier must encode a maximum likelihood estimate of the ground truth in its latent state, leading to abstract and disentangled representations as the number of tasks increases.
RNNs trained on multi-task classification learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, enabling zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization.
Transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, achieving orthogonality even with fewer tasks compared to RNNs.
Noise in observations is necessary for disentangled representations to emerge, as it prevents saturation and preserves distance information.
The framework is robust to various manipulations including correlated inputs, non-linear decision boundaries, and free reaction-time tasks.
future_direction: Characterizing representation learning with multiple manifold decision boundaries
Exploring interplay between task diversity, energy constraints, and the emergence of shared representations
papers.abstract: Intelligent perception and interaction with the world hinges on internal representations that capture its underlying structure (''disentangled'' or ''abstract'' representations). Disentangled representations serve as world models, isolating latent factors of variation in the world along approximately orthogonal directions, thus facilitating feature-based generalization. We provide experimental and theoretical results guaranteeing the emergence of disentangled representations in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks, canonical in the neuroscience literature. The key conceptual finding is that, by producing accurate multi-task classification estimates, a system implicitly represents a set of coordinates specifying a disentangled representation of the underlying latent state of the data it receives. The theory provides conditions for the emergence of these representations in terms of noise, number of tasks, and evidence accumulation time. We experimentally validate these predictions in RNNs trained to multi-task, which learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, leading to zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in predicting latent factors. We demonstrate the robustness of our framework across autoregressive architectures, decision boundary geometries and in tasks requiring classification confidence estimation. We find that transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, which might explain their unique world understanding abilities. Overall, our framework establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, and helps explain why ANNs often arrive at human-interpretable concepts, and how they both may acquire exceptional zero-shot generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Decomposing multimodal embedding spaces with group-sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to adapt sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for multimodal embeddings to mitigate the tradeoff between monosemanticity and modality alignment.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a group-sparse autoencoder with cross-modal random masking to learn multimodal dictionaries from aligned embeddings, improving modality alignment, reducing dead neurons, and enhancing feature semanticity compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: The proposed group-sparse autoencoder with cross-modal random masking learns dictionaries with better multimodal alignment, fewer dead neurons, and improved semanticity, enabling better interpretability and control in cross-modal tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MGSAE increases the number of neurons that activate for both modalities and reduces dead neurons.
MGSAE improves multimodal monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAEs.
MGSAE improves zero-shot performance on cross-modal tasks like image/text and audio/text classification and retrieval.
The method enables better interpretability, e.g., in concept naming for linear probes on attributes like 'blonde hair'.
The approach generalizes to different multimodal encoders (SIGLIP2, AIMv2) and datasets (MS COCO).
papers.abstract: The Linear Representation Hypothesis asserts that the embeddings learned by neural networks can be understood as linear combinations of features corresponding to high-level concepts. Based on this ansatz, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become a popular method for decomposing embeddings into a sparse combination of linear directions, which have been shown empirically to often correspond to human-interpretable semantics. However, recent attempts to apply SAEs to multimodal embedding spaces (such as the popular CLIP embeddings for image/text data) have found that SAEs often learn "split dictionaries", where most of the learned sparse features are essentially unimodal, active only for data of a single modality. In this work, we study how to effectively adapt SAEs for the setting of multimodal embeddings while ensuring multimodal alignment. We first argue that the existence of a split dictionary decomposition on an aligned embedding space implies the existence of a non-split dictionary with improved modality alignment. Then, we propose a new SAE-based approach to multimodal embedding decomposition using cross-modal random masking and group-sparse regularization. We apply our method to popular embeddings for image/text (CLIP) and audio/text (CLAP) data and show that, compared to standard SAEs, our approach learns a more multimodal dictionary while reducing the number of dead neurons and improving feature semanticity. We finally demonstrate how this improvement in alignment of concepts between modalities can enable improvements in the interpretability and control of cross-modal tasks.

papers.title: Do LLMs and VLMs Share Neurons for Inference? Evidence and Mechanisms of Cross-Modal Transfer
papers.research_question: Do LLMs and VLMs share neurons for inference? Can we leverage the mature capabilities of LLMs to enhance LVLMs at low cost?
papers.core_contribution: This work discovers a shared neuron subspace between LLMs and LVLMs and introduces SNRF, a parameter-efficient framework that transfers mature inference circuitry from LLMs to LVLMs by selectively updating shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers a shared neuron subspace between LLMs and LVLMs, showing that many of the most active neurons overlap across modalities and encode causal, concept-level semantics. Leveraging this insight, SNRF transfers mature textual abilities into LVLMs by selectively aligning and updating these shared neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Different series of VL models and their corresponding text-math models share a large number of neurons on inference tasks.
Shared inference basis plays an important role in a model’s performance on inference tasks.
A large portion of shared neurons are linked to math inference.
SNRF consistently improves LVLM inference performance while preserving perceptual capabilities.
Shared neurons encode consistent and interpretable concept-level effects, demonstrating their functional contribution to inference.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have rapidly advanced across various domains, yet they still lag behind strong text-only large language models (LLMs) on tasks that require multi-step inference and compositional decision-making. Motivated by their shared transformer architectures, we investigate whether the two model families rely on common internal computation for such inference. At the neuron level, we uncover a surprisingly large overlap: more than half of the top-activated units during multi-step inference are shared between representative LLMs and LVLMs, revealing a modality-invariant inference subspace. Through causal probing via activation amplification, we further show that these shared neurons encode consistent and interpretable concept-level effects, demonstrating their functional contribution to inference. Building on this insight, we propose Shared Neuron Low-Rank Fusion (SNRF), a parameter-efficient framework that transfers mature inference circuitry from LLMs to LVLMs. SNRF profiles cross-model activations to identify shared neurons, computes a low-rank approximation of inter-model weight differences, and injects these updates selectively within the shared-neuron subspace. This mechanism strengthens multimodal inference performance with minimal parameter changes and requires no large-scale multimodal fine-tuning. Across diverse mathematics and perception benchmarks, SNRF consistently enhances LVLM inference performance while preserving perceptual capabilities. Our results demonstrate that shared neurons form an interpretable bridge between LLMs and LVLMs, enabling low-cost transfer of inference ability into multimodal models. Our code is available at [https://github.com/chenhangcuisg-code/Do-LLMs-VLMs-Share-Neurons](https://github.com/chenhangcuisg-code/Do-LLMs-VLMs-Share-Neurons).

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Uncovering Grounding IDs: How External Cues Shape Multimodal Binding
papers.research_question: Why do external cues improve reasoning in large vision-language models (LVLMs)? The paper investigates how external visual and textual cues induce latent identifiers (Grounding IDs) that improve cross-modal alignment and reduce hallucinations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that external visual and textual cues induce latent identifiers (Grounding IDs) in LVLMs, which enhance cross-modal alignment, reduce hallucinations, and improve visual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Grounding IDs are a key mechanism for partition-based binding, providing mechanistic insight into how external cues improve multimodal grounding and reasoning in LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
External cues (symbols, grid lines) improve attention within partitions and cross-modal alignment.
Grounding IDs emerge as latent vectors that bind visual and textual tokens belonging to the same partition.
Activation swapping experiments show that object-symbol bindings are mediated by Grounding IDs, not local features.
Grounding IDs reduce the modality gap between visual and textual representations.
Structured inputs reduce hallucinations in long caption generation and improve performance on visual reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation: Structured inputs may have lower recall in object presence questions due to objects spanning grid boundaries or being positioned across partitions.
future_direction: Discovering circuits that support system-2 reasoning tasks, such as counting and spatial reasoning.
Integrating external cues during RL finetuning to strengthen the model's internal ability to perform sequential scanning based on provided cues.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) show strong performance across multimodal benchmarks but remain limited in structured reasoning and precise grounding. Recent work has demonstrated that adding simple visual structures, such as partitions and annotations, improves accuracy, yet the internal mechanisms underlying these gains remain unclear. We investigate this phenomenon and propose the concept of Grounding IDs, latent identifiers induced by external cues that bind objects to their designated partitions across modalities. Through representation analysis, we find that these identifiers emerge as consistent within-partition alignment in embedding space and reduce the modality gap between image and text. Causal interventions further confirm that these identifiers mediate binding between objects and symbolic cues. We show that Grounding IDs strengthen attention between related components, which in turn improves cross-modal grounding and reduces hallucinations. Taken together, our results identify Grounding IDs as a key symbolic mechanism that explains how external cues enhance multimodal binding and offer both interpretability and practical improvements.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Brain-to-Speech Models Across Speech Modes
papers.research_question: How do brain-to-speech decoding models internally represent and transfer information across different speech modes (vocalized, mimed, imagined)?
papers.core_contribution: Speech modes lie on a shared continuous causal manifold, and cross-mode transfer is mediated by compact, layer-specific subspaces rather than diffuse activity.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can uncover the internal representations that causally support speech decoding and clarify how these representations differ across speech modes, leading to more predictable, controllable, and robust models.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-mode activation patching shows vocalized internal states are sufficient to recover high-quality decoding on imagined and mimed inputs, while the reverse causes performance collapse.
Tri-modal activation interpolation shows smooth transitions, indicating a shared continuous causal manifold across speech modes.
Causal localization identifies specific convolutional channels and recurrent time windows that mediate cross-mode transfer.
Neuron-level analysis reveals cross-modal transfer relies on small subsets of neurons, not single neurons or broad populations.
Causal scrubbing confirms that the identified subspaces are sufficient for transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to one model architecture and one dataset, so findings may not generalize to other models or datasets.
future_direction: Check if the identified convolutional and recurrent bottlenecks remain when using other sequence models (e.g., LSTMs, transformers, state-space models) and with more subjects and datasets.
Study how the identified subspaces develop during training.
Train models to encourage imagined and mimed inputs to use the same internal subspaces that support accurate vocalized decoding.
papers.abstract: Brain-to-speech decoding models demonstrate robust performance in vocalized, mimed, and imagined speech; yet, the fundamental mechanisms via which these models capture and transmit information across different speech modalities are less explored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability to causally investigate the internal representations of a neural speech decoder. We perform cross-mode activation patching of internal activations across speech modes, and use tri-modal interpolation to examine whether speech representations vary discretely or continuously. We use coarse-to-fine causal tracing and causal scrubbing to find localized causal structure, allowing us to find internal subspaces that are sufficient for cross-mode transfer. In order to determine how finely distributed these effects are within layers, we perform neuron-level activation patching. We discover that small but not distributed subsets of neurons, rather than isolated units, affect the cross-mode transfer. Our results show that speech modes lie on a shared continuous causal manifold, and cross-mode transfer is mediated by compact, layer-specific subspaces rather than diffuse activity. Together, our findings give a causal explanation for how speech modality information is organized and used in brain-to-speech decoding models, revealing hierarchical and direction-dependent representational structure across speech modes.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Investigating Inner Properties of Multimodal Representation and Semantic Compositionality with Brain-based Componential Semantics
papers.research_question: What properties are encoded in multimodal representations, in what aspects do they outperform single-modality representations, and how does semantic compositionality work in different input modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses brain-based componential semantics to investigate inner properties of multimodal representations and semantic compositionality, finding that multimodal models improve on sensory/motor properties but degrade on abstract properties, and that semantic compositionality is a general process across modalities with the Matrix model performing best.
papers.conclusion: The results shed light on the potential of combining representations from different modalities, building better multimodal models by distinguishing different types of concepts, and learning semantic compositionality in multimodal environment.
papers.key_findings:
Single modality vectors from different sources encode complementary semantics, giving multimodal models the potential to better represent concept meanings.
Multimodal models improve text-based models on sensory and motor properties, but degrade the representation quality of abstract properties.
Different input modalities have similar effects on inner properties of semantic representations when combining words into phrases, indicating that semantic compositionality is a general process irrespective of input modalities.
Different composition models combine the inner properties of constituent word representations in different ways, and the Matrix model best simulates semantic compositionality in multimodal environment.
Perceptual input may not be valuable for abstract concepts in building multimodal models.
papers.limitation: Auditory inputs greatly decrease model performance, so only linguistic and visual inputs are used for multimodal vectors.
papers.abstract: Multimodal models have been proven to outperform text-based approaches on learning semantic representations. However, it still remains unclear what properties are encoded in multimodal representations, in what aspects do they outperform the single-modality representations, and what happened in the process of semantic compositionality in different input modalities. Considering that multimodal models are originally motivated by human concept representations, we assume that correlating multimodal representations with brain-based semantics would interpret their inner properties to answer the above questions. To that end, we propose simple interpretation methods based on brain-based componential semantics. First we investigate the inner properties of multimodal representations by correlating them with corresponding brain-based property vectors. Then we map the distributed vector space to the interpretable brain-based componential space to explore the inner properties of semantic compositionality. Ultimately, the present paper sheds light on the fundamental questions of natural language understanding, such as how to represent the meaning of words and how to combine word meanings into larger units.

papers.title: Synergistic information supports modality integration and flexible learning in neural networks solving multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How and why synergistic information emerges in cognitive systems, and how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations, while synergistic information supports the integration of multiple modalities and enables flexible and efficient learning in neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Synergistic information is crucial for general-purpose learning as it supports integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning, while redundant information provides robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks.
Performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons.
Dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness.
Synergy is specifically linked to the integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning.
Redundant information provides robustness but is less efficient.
future_direction: Future work may seek to disentangle the relevance of each potential cause driving the importance of synergistic neurons.
Empirical evaluation of the conjectures about unique information in specialized circuits is an interesting avenue.
papers.abstract: Striking progress has recently been made in understanding human cognition by analyzing how its neuronal underpinnings are engaged in different modes of information processing. Specifically, neural information can be decomposed into synergistic, redundant, and unique features, with synergistic components being particularly aligned with complex cognition. However, two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (a) precisely how and why a cognitive system can become highly synergistic; and (b) how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes. To address these questions, here we employ an information-decomposition framework to investigate the information processing strategies adopted by simple artificial neural networks performing a variety of cognitive tasks in both supervised and reinforcement learning settings. Our results show that synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks. Furthermore, performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons. Finally, randomly turning off neurons during training through dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness. Overall, our results suggest that while redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations in the learning process, synergistic information is used to combine information from multiple modalities -- and more generally for flexible and efficient learning. These findings open the door to new ways of investigating how and why learning systems employ specific information-processing strategies, and support the principle that the capacity for general-purpose learning critically relies in the system's information dynamics.

papers.title: Untangling in Invariant Speech Recognition
papers.research_question: How do deep neural networks for speech recognition untangle task-relevant information (e.g., words, phonemes) and discard nuisance variations (e.g., speaker identity) across layers and over time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that deep speech recognition models untangle task-relevant auditory class manifolds (e.g., words, phonemes) and discard nuisance variations (e.g., speaker identity) across layers, and that this untangling emerges from training and is consistent across different network architectures.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks for speech recognition untangle auditory class manifolds in a manner analogous to vision networks, and geometric analysis of representations reveals how invariant speech recognition is achieved.
papers.key_findings:
Word manifolds become more linearly separable (higher manifold capacity) in later layers of both CNN and Deep Speech 2 models.
Higher-level concepts such as phonemes and parts-of-speech also become untangled in later layers, though to a lesser extent than words.
Speaker information (speaker manifolds) is discarded in models trained for speech recognition, as evidenced by decreased manifold capacity for speaker manifolds in later layers.
Temporal untangling occurs over time steps in recurrent layers, with word separability peaking near the word's temporal location.
The untangling is task-dependent: models trained for speaker recognition untangle speaker manifolds but not word manifolds.
future_direction: Theory-driven geometric analysis of representation untangling in tasks with temporal structure.
Search for the mechanistic relation between the network architecture, learned parameters, and structure of the stimuli via the lens of geometry.
Study of competing vs. synergistic tasks enabled by the geometric analysis tool.
papers.abstract: Encouraged by the success of deep neural networks on a variety of visual tasks, much theoretical and experimental work has been aimed at understanding and interpreting how vision networks operate. Meanwhile, deep neural networks have also achieved impressive performance in audio processing applications, both as sub-components of larger systems and as complete end-to-end systems by themselves. Despite their empirical successes, comparatively little is understood about how these audio models accomplish these tasks. In this work, we employ a recently developed statistical mechanical theory that connects geometric properties of network representations and the separability of classes to probe how information is untangled within neural networks trained to recognize speech. We observe that speaker-specific nuisance variations are discarded by the network's hierarchy, whereas task-relevant properties such as words and phonemes are untangled in later layers. Higher level concepts such as parts-of-speech and context dependence also emerge in the later layers of the network. Finally, we find that the deep representations carry out significant temporal untangling by efficiently extracting task-relevant features at each time step of the computation. Taken together, these findings shed light on how deep auditory models process time dependent input signals to achieve invariant speech recognition, and show how different concepts emerge through the layers of the network.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How do individual CNN features from all layers behave for feature extraction and transfer learning, and can both presence and absence of feature activations be informative?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both presence and absence, and that convolutional layers are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the behavior of CNN features for feature extraction, showing that both presence and absence of features are informative, and that convolutional layers are more general than previously thought, which can be exploited for knowledge representation and reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their absence, providing a different information modality, especially in fine-grained datasets.
Features from the last convolutional layer and fully connected layers are highly specific, while other convolutional layers convey more variate information.
For certain tasks, convolutional features outperform fully-connected features at discriminating labels, indicating low-level layers are more general and discriminant.
Low and middle level features have similar behavior across datasets, suggesting they can be used for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly related to the similarity of the task with the original training task and the width of the task spectrum.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Create Cross-Modal Task Representations
papers.research_question: Do vision-language models (VLMs) map conceptually equivalent inputs (across modalities and formats) into a shared task representation?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs map conceptually equivalent inputs (text examples, image examples, instructions) into a shared task representation, and cross-modal patching of this single task vector can effectively transfer task information across modalities.
papers.conclusion: VLMs map inputs into a shared task representation space regardless of specification modality or format, and cross-modal patching is an effective method for analyzing and utilizing these representations.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs struggle with cross-modal few-shot prompting (input regurgitation), but cross-modal patching of a task vector resolves this issue and often outperforms unimodal baselines.
Task vectors can be transferred from a base language model (LLM) to its fine-tuned vision-language counterpart (VLM), indicating representational re-use.
Task vectors can be defined solely from instructions, and ensembling instruction- and example-based vectors improves sample efficiency.
VLMs map text and image examples (and instructions) to similar task vectors, despite maintaining distinct image and text embeddings in the context.
The token representation evolution during in-context learning follows three phases (input, task, answer) that are shared across text and image ICL.
papers.limitation:
The work shows that VLMs learn cross-modal task representations but lacks a definitive explanation for why.
The reliability of these models remains a limitation; task adaptation often comes at the cost of accuracy, requiring further stress testing before deployment in critical applications.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) can handle many tasks within a single model, yet the representations that enable this capability remain opaque. We find that VLMs align conceptually equivalent inputs into a shared task vector, which is invariant to modality (text, image) and format (examples, instruction), and may simplify VLM processing. We measure this alignment via cross-modal transfer -- the ability of a task vector derived in one modality to trigger the correct generation in another -- on a range of tasks and model architectures. Although the task vector is highly compressed, we find that this single vector outperforms prompting the model with the full task information, unique to this cross-modal case. Furthermore, we show that task vectors can be transferred from a base language model to its fine-tuned vision-language counterpart, and that they can be derived solely from instructions without the need for examples. Taken together, our findings shed light on how VLMs internally process task information, and how they map different modalities into common semantic representations. Project page: https://vlm-cross-modal-reps.github.io.

papers.title: Disentangled Representations in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations in neural models that are interpretable, reusable, and performant, without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods (DC-IGN and CFN) for learning disentangled representations in graphics and computation, which are interpretable, reusable, and performant without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled representations are valuable for interpretability and reuse, and the proposed methods (DC-IGN and CFN) are effective in learning such representations in the domains of graphics and computation.
papers.key_findings:
DC-IGN can learn a disentangled graphics code for 3D faces and chairs, enabling novel view synthesis and re-rendering under different lighting and pose conditions.
CFN can disentangle computational tasks, factorize a multitask learning problem, and is practically immune to catastrophic forgetting.
Explicit disentanglement training is critical for novel-view reconstruction compared to entangled representations.
The decoder in DC-IGN can function as a 3D rendering engine, indicating a truly disentangled representation.
CFN achieves disentanglement with no performance penalty and with fewer parameters than a traditional feedforward network.
papers.limitation:
The current formulation of SGVB is restricted to continuous latent variables, but real-world scenes may require discrete distributions.
Scaling to more complex scenes may require deeper architectures.
The decoder network might be replaced by a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained model-based inference.
future_direction: Experiment with deeper architectures to handle more complex scenes and object categories.
Extend the model to handle discrete distributions or to a recurrent setting.
Use importance-weighted autoencoders to capture more complex probabilistic structure.
Replace the decoder with a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained inference.
Explore multi-step CFN for deeper computations and curricula.
Investigate non-differentiable functions in CFN and hierarchical computation.
Unify the two approaches for unsupervised inference of factors of variation in videos.
papers.abstract: Representation learning is the foundation for the recent success of neural network models. However, the distributed representations generated by neural networks are far from ideal. Due to their highly entangled nature, they are di cult to reuse and interpret, and they do a poor job of capturing the sparsity which is present in real- world transformations. In this paper, I describe methods for learning disentangled representations in the two domains of graphics and computation. These methods allow neural methods to learn representations which are easy to interpret and reuse, yet they incur little or no penalty to performance. In the Graphics section, I demonstrate the ability of these methods to infer the generating parameters of images and rerender those images under novel conditions. In the Computation section, I describe a model which is able to factorize a multitask learning problem into subtasks and which experiences no catastrophic forgetting. Together these techniques provide the tools to design a wide range of models that learn disentangled representations and better model the factors of variation in the real world.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Unsupervised learning in images and audio to produce neural receptive fields: a primer and accessible notebook
papers.research_question: How can unsupervised learning, specifically Independent Component Analysis (ICA), model early sensory processing in vision and audition, and how does it compare to Principal Component Analysis (PCA)?
